segments.transcript: The approach to bone specimens depends on why bone is present in the specimen. One scenario is when the primary diagnosis is not bone; bone is simply present, such as in a mandible with squamous cell carcinoma where the carcinoma is invading the bone. In this case, the definitive diagnosis does not typically rely on bone sections, although stage or margins might, which can often be addressed with a single slide. The other, more common scenario, especially in certain contexts, is when the primary diagnosis *is* bone. Here, not only do stage and margins depend on the bone, but determining the tumor type itself relies on bone sections, making it a far more complex process. The simpler scenario will be discussed first.

segments.transcript: Bone diagnoses utilize a variety of specimen types, ranging from Fine Needle Aspiration (FNA) and core biopsy, primarily for diagnosis, to larger procedures for both diagnosis and therapy. Procedures like curettage are analogous to marginal excisions, used to debulk tumors and often serve for both diagnosis and therapy, sometimes involving a frozen section. Wider excisions, where a segment of bone is removed, limb-sparing procedures, which involve removing an entire bone and inserting a prosthesis to save the limb, and ultimately amputation, are performed for therapeutic purposes. An incisional biopsy can also be therapeutic if the lesion is benign, requiring no further treatment. There is an additional step for primary bone pathology specimens. In addition to reviewing prior pathology in Apex and CoPath, similar to soft tissue, correlation with imaging is crucial. This is particularly important for neoplastic lesions, providing context on the bone's identity, its relation to normal anatomy, and the tumor's location within the specimen, which might not be externally visible. Imaging also assists with complex cases like diabetic feet, where disaggregated bones can be difficult to identify and orient. Pre- and post-operative films are almost always available. For example, if the distal part of the first metatarsal was removed, imaging helps confirm what you are holding and its orientation, saving significant time. The same considerations for measurements and special processing issues apply as with soft tissue specimens.

segments.transcript: The tumor's name, myxofibrosarcoma, derives from 'myxo' coming first because it is predominantly myxoid. However, fibromyxoid sarcoma starts with 'fibro' instead of 'myxo,' indicating it is predominantly collagenous and pink, with some alternating myxoid zones. This distinction is important as the former is typically blue and myxoid, while fibromyxoid sarcoma is pink. Fibromyxoid sarcoma is common in younger patients, including children and those in their 20s and 30s, although it can occur across all age groups. Myxofibrosarcoma, conversely, is more common in older adults. If a tumor appears to be either myxofibrosarcoma or fibromyxoid sarcoma and is found in a young patient, it is likely fibromyxoid sarcoma. These tumors can occur in extremities but also in unusual locations like the pelvis or thorax. They are deep, intramuscular lesions, not subcutaneous, and are infiltrating. Unlike superficial cutaneous masses that may be excised without imaging, these deep-seated lesions typically require an MRI to assess their infiltration and guide surgical resection, which may involve removing surrounding muscle.

segments.transcript: Acute osteomyelitis can present with diabetic toes or osteomyelitis in children, and it's a diagnosis that should be made with imaging and clinical correlation. Clinically, it's a diverse disease: children typically don't have classic infection symptoms like fever or elevated white counts, while diabetic toe infections are more obvious with gangrene and pus. Radiographically, acute osteomyelitis is typically lytic and permeative. In children with growth plates, the infection is confined to the epiphysis or metaphysis, not crossing the physis due to separate blood supplies. However, in infants without growth plates and adults with closed growth plates, the infection can spread to the diaphysis. Histologically, the diagnosis is made by finding sheets of neutrophils in the marrow space, along with dead bone (sequestrum) or scalloped bone surfaces. The body's healing response involves new bone formation called involucrum. Differential diagnoses include Langerhans cell histiocytosis and fractures, requiring clinical history to differentiate.

segments.transcript: Paget's disease of bone is one of the most common bone lesions seen in adults. It is not a neoplasm, nor is it technically a metabolic disease because it is not ongoing. Patients with Paget's disease do not develop new lesions after the initial diagnosis; existing lesions remain the only ones they will ever have. It is likely related to both an autoimmune process and potentially an infection. The pathology of the disease depends on when it is detected. It is most often caught in a sporadic phase, typically when a patient is being evaluated for something else, such as surveillance for metastatic prostate cancer, which often affects the vertebral bodies. These lesions are usually asymptomatic and found incidentally. Paget's disease can occasionally be picked up in an earlier, active phase with osteoblastic activity, or in the very earliest phase, which is purely lytic, though this is rare. The lytic phase involves increased osteoclast activity, similar to hyperparathyroidism, while the sclerotic phase shows increased bone and abnormal reversal cement lines. This is the sclerotic phase, the skull that's diffusely involved at Paget's. Too much bone, too much matrix, and too much calcium. segments.transcript: As a pathologist, you are not trained to read films. However, as a physician, you should be able to at least look at a plain film, identify a lesion, and describe it. At a minimum, you should be able to read a radiology report, understand the descriptions, and know what the words mean. This does not mean you need to be able to read an MRI with all its different modalities, but plain X-rays and CT scans are likely important. For bone lesions, a plain X-ray often requires two views, at 90-degree orthogonal angles, to properly visualize the lesion, as one view might not show it well due to bone penetration. These two views provide 90% of the diagnosis. CT scans are helpful, especially for axial skeleton lesions like the vertebral body or pelvis, where multiple tissue layers can obscure lesions on plain films. Permeative lesions, which fill the marrow cavity without destroying or forming new bone (like lymphoma), may not be visible on plain X-rays as they don't alter the calcium content. CT scans offer higher sensitivity and can distinguish between fat and soft tissue densities. MRI is more complex due to its various modalities and contrast options, but it is useful for planning surgery and identifying soft tissue components. If a lesion is not seen on a plain X-ray, MRI can help determine if it's a bone tumor or a soft tissue tumor eroding into bone. While useful, understanding the nuances of MRI is not strictly required for all physicians. For plain films, physicians should be able to understand the terminology used by radiologists and look for opacity, the border of the lesion, and any periosteal reaction.

segments.transcript: Hyaline cartilage is a common primary bone tumor, comprising 65% water, 15% proteoglycan (aggrecan, chondroitin sulfate side chain), 15% collagen (mostly type 2), and less than 5% cells. Fibrocartilage has more collagen and is never neoplastic, while elastic cartilage has more elastin and is also never neoplastic. Permeation, described as the "oozing" of cartilage matrix and cells around viable lamellar bone, is a key indicator of malignancy in cartilage tumors. Atypia, referring to nucleomegaly and visible nuclear detail, increased N/C ratio, and nucleoli in chondrocytes, is also a sign of malignancy. Nesting, defined as more than one cell per lacune, and clustering, where cells group into packets separated by acellular zones, can be seen in benign processes, including osteoarthritis. Binucleation, or more than one nucleus per cell, is mentioned as a soft feature for malignancy in cartilage tumors, though its specificity is debated.

segments.transcript: Ewing sarcoma is an undifferentiated small round blue cell tumor. Unlike other sarcomas that produce matrix, such as chondrosarcoma producing cartilage or osteosarcoma producing bone, Ewing sarcoma is devoid of matrix, appearing as sheets of undifferentiated cells. Classically, it was described as forming Homer Wright rosettes, where cells radiate from a central core of neuropil. While true Homer Wright rosettes are rare in Ewing sarcoma, they can occasionally occur. The term P-NET, or primitive neuroectodermal tumor, was historically used due to evidence of neuroectodermal origin and formation of neuropil-like structures. However, with the realization that these are all Ewing sarcomas characterized by the EWSR1-FLI1 fusion, P-NET is no longer a distinct diagnosis. Immunohistochemistry is useful, but genetics will be discussed further.

For low-power architecture, you can appreciate the difference between DCIS and atypical ductal hyperplasia (ADH). DCIS shows a more rigid architecture at low power, best appreciated when forming secondary spaces; these will be more cribriform and irregular. ADH will show at least some of this rigid architecture, while UDH (without a TPR) will have irregular architecture. Therefore, you can get an idea whether the lesion is typical or atypical just by looking at low-power architecture. Then, you'll go to high power to appreciate the cytology. DCIS is a neoplastic lesion, so the cells are very much alike—uniform, with round to slightly ovoid nuclei, and they respect each other. They're very tidy and organized, resulting in distinct cell borders. UDH, on the other hand, is not a neoplastic process; it comprises a heterogeneous population. The cells look very different, overlapping nuclei on top of each other, creating a kind of 'jungle' appearance. This helps differentiate typical from atypical proliferative lesions.

segments.transcript: So, even given this type of problem, how do we approach it? We can categorize ADH into two types. One is qualitatively insufficient, or "mimic DCIS." These cases show partial involvement of the duct by atypical cells, as defined for low-grade DCIS (LG DCIS). The other is quantitatively insufficient, or "mini DCIS." This occurs when all the cytologic and architectural features of LG DCIS are present, but the involvement is less than two spaces or less than or equal to two millimeters in extent. This is because a DCIS diagnosis can be psychologically traumatizing for patients, and it often comes with recommendations for radiation and hormonal therapy, which have complications. Therefore, quantitatively insufficient cases, where the features are present but the extent is too small, are better termed atypical ductal hyperplasia rather than DCIS.

segments.transcript: It is important to understand how to differentiate low-grade ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) from usual ductal hyperplasia (UDH). High-grade DCIS has obvious cytologic features, making differentiation less problematic. The challenge lies in separating low-grade DCIS from UDH. Their architectures differ significantly. Cribriform spaces in DCIS are round and punched out, whereas in UDH they are often irregular. Rigid bars and arcades, club-shaped micropapillae, and solid patterns can be seen in both, offering less diagnostic value. However, cytologic features such as uniform, evenly spaced, and highly organized nuclei with distinct cell borders are more helpful in identifying DCIS, often resembling a tiled pattern, especially under altered condenser settings. In addition to architectural and cytologic features, size and extent are crucial. Page (1985) criteria suggest involvement of at least two duct spaces, while Tavassoli (1990) proposes a minimum of 2mm extent. Most pathologists prefer to avoid diagnosing DCIS if the area is small, instead classifying it as UDH. This is because a small region of low-grade DCIS is better categorized as UDH.

High-grade DCIS typically shows pleomorphic or linear branching (casting) calcifications, while low- and intermediate-grade DCIS tends to present with granular or amorphous calcifications. Rarely, DCIS may present as a palpable mass, particularly in high-grade cases or those involving underlying lesions such as papilloma or sclerosing adenosis. Patients may also experience nipple discharge or Paget disease of the nipple. Approximately 5% of DCIS cases are incidental findings discovered during a biopsy, sometimes alongside other lesions. On MRI, DCIS can manifest as non-mass linear enhancement, often detected in high-risk patients undergoing screening. These findings are usually discovered when the patient has a high-risk factor or is being screened. The MRI helps to assess the extent of the region. Grossly, no obvious lesion is seen because it's just starting, and then with the classification, you won't be able to recognize it. However, high-grade extensive DCIS can present as a palpable mass. segments.transcript: It's a distribution of DCIS. Multi centricity, or involvement of different regions (usually different quadrants) of the breast, is very relevant to management. LCIS very often is multicentric; it can involve all parts of the breast and uncommonly, both breasts. However, multicentric involvement in DCIS is very rare. A 1994 study by Holland and Hendriks analyzed 119 mastectomy specimens and found only one case not confined to a single segment. Basically, DCIS is a continuous lesion, not multicentric, except in rare cases. Pure micropapillary, not mixed micropapillary DCIS, shows a higher frequency of non-segmental or multicentric distribution. This is important for treatment. The natural history of DCIS is largely unknown because it is typically excised. However, studies of patients initially diagnosed with and untreated DCIS provide insight. DCIS is a non-obligate precursor to invasive breast cancer; up to 50% recur as invasive cancers. However, not all cases recur. Hybrid recurrences occur more frequently and quickly. When invasive cancer develops from DCIS, it's usually in the same breast and side. Genetic studies show that DCIS and invasive breast cancer share similar genetic profiles. Therefore, the goal of treatment is complete excision. If it is segmental, excision is possible; if multicentric, mastectomy is indicated.

segments.transcript: How to stratify patients with regard to treatment? Patients with the lowest risk of recurrence may undergo local excision. Those with a high risk of recurrence may require a mastectomy. Intermediate-risk patients may receive local excision, with or without XRT and/or tamoxifen. Clinical features associated with local recurrence in ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) include young age (under 40 years), high mammographic density, symptomatic disease (palpable tumor detected before mammography), multifocal disease or large tumor size, family history of breast cancer, and treatment category. Histopathologic features include high nuclear grade, comedo necrosis, tumor size, and involvement of or close surgical margins. Biomarkers such as ER, HER2, and cell cycle markers (Ki67, p53, COX-2, p16), along with multiparameter molecular assays, also contribute to recurrence prediction. Dimension, size, the larger the more likely, and the closer margin. In addition to those factors, other elements influence the outcome. Clinical features related to local recurrence in DCIS include young age (less than 40 years), high mammographic density, symptomatic disease (palpable and detectable by more than mammography alone), multifocal disease or large tumor size, family history of DCIS, and treatment category. Histopathologic features include high nuclear grade, comedo necrosis, tumor size, and the involvement or proximity of the surgical margin. Biomarkers such as ER, HER2, and cell cycle markers (Ki67, p53, COX-2, p16), as well as multiparameter molecular assays, are also correlated with recurrence. Evidence is shown here for your reference. The table displays recurrence rates based on nuclear grade. Low-grade DCIS has an 8.1% recurrence rate with CS and a 3.7% recurrence rate with CS + RT. Intermediate-grade DCIS shows a 22.7% recurrence rate with CS and 7.5% with CS + RT. High-grade DCIS has a 23% recurrence rate with CS and 9.5% with CS + RT. This data is from Boyages J et al., A meta-analysis. Cancer 1999;85:61. One study uses what we call the Van Nuys Prognostic Index. This is initially measured using mammography (looking for calcifications). Pathologic evaluation, the gold standard, involves total and serial sequential sampling (SSS or mapping), the block number multiplied by block thickness (block method), or the largest extent on a single slide. The report should include the size and method used.

segments.transcript: The Van Nuys prognostic index scoring system (M. Silverstein et al., Cancer 1996;77:2267-74) uses a scoring system based on tumor size, margin width, and pathologic classification. Scores range from 1 to 3, with higher scores indicating a worse prognosis. The criteria for size are ≤15 mm, 16-40 mm, and >41 mm; margin width criteria are >10 mm, 1-9 mm, and <1 mm; and pathologic classifications are nonhigh grade with or without necrosis, nonhigh grade with necrosis, and high grade with or without necrosis. The updated Van Nuys Prognostic Index (VNPI) for DCI includes age. Each factor—size (mm), margin width (mm), pathologic classification (grade), and age—is assigned points. Higher point totals indicate higher risk. Scores are categorized as 1, 2, or 3, with 3 representing the highest risk. The VNPI score helps determine the appropriate treatment for ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS). A VNPI score of 4-6 indicates low risk and may be treated with excision only. A score of 7-9 indicates intermediate risk, with radiation therapy (XRT) recommended. A score of 10-12 indicates high risk, and a mastectomy should be considered. Active surveillance trials of low-risk DCIS include the Loris trial in the UK (Surgery Versus Active Monitoring for Low-Risk DCIS), the Lord trial in continental Europe (Management of Low-Risk DCIS), the Comet trial in the USA (Comparison of Operative Monitoring and Endocrine Therapy for low-risk DCIS), and the Loretta trial in Japan.

segments.transcript: Juvenile fibroadenoma is a special morphological type with a constellation of features. It is more common in women under 20 years old; however, the usual-type fibroadenoma is most common in all age groups. Juvenile fibroadenomas can mimic phyllodes tumors clinically and morphologically due to rapid growth and large size. Histological features that may cause concern for phyllodes tumors include cellular stroma, pericanalicular growth, and lobular architecture. 'Gynecomastoid'/micropapillary usual ductal hyperplasia may also be present, as well as stromal mitotic activity (rarely up to 6/10 high-power fields). However, stromal cytologic atypia is absent, and the cellularity and epithelial:stromal distribution are uniform. Treatment involves excision with preservation of adjacent breast tissue, crucial for adolescent patients due to ongoing breast development. Simple excision is preferred to avoid affecting breast development.

segments.transcript: Phyllodes tumors are fibroepithelial neoplasms showing a prominent intracanalicular architectural pattern with leaf-like stromal fronds. These fronds are capped by luminal epithelial and myoepithelial cell layers, as expected for benign epithelial components, and are accompanied by stromal hypercellularity. Phyllodes tumors are rare, comprising less than 1% of primary breast tumors and less than 2.5% of fibroepithelial lesions in tertiary centers. The average age of diagnosis is 40-50 years, but there is a wide range, from adolescence to 90 years old. Patients with phyllodes tumors are, on average, 15-20 years older than those with fibroadenomas. Benign phyllodes tumors tend to present at a younger age than borderline or malignant phyllodes tumors. Phyllodes tumors are more common in Asian and Latina women, who may present with the tumor at a younger age. There is an increased incidence of phyllodes tumors in patients with Li-Fraumeni syndrome, which is associated with TP53 gene mutations. These tumors can be bilateral or multiple.

Large tumors can cause skin ulceration. The mean size is 4–5 cm, but there is a wide range (less than 3 cm to 20+ cm). Smaller lesions are increasingly detected by screening. Imaging is not accurate in differentiating between phyllodes tumors (PT) and fibroadenomas (FA), and it is not reliable in grading phyllodes tumors. Typically, phyllodes tumors and fibroadenomas present as oval, lobulated lesions that are hypoechoic. This is a phyllodes tumor, and with internal hyperechoic striations. If you see internal hyperechoic striations, it is usually a little more concerning to be a phyllodes tumor than a phylloma. Growth features of phyllodes tumors are mostly circumscribed and have shelled-out borders. Many benign phyllodes tumors, upon surgical excision, appear to be easily shelled out. Malignant phyllodes tumors, however, are often more infiltrative and have a bosselated cut surface. Cystic spaces or elongated clefts may be present, along with leaf-like projections. segments.transcript: Okay, so once you decide this is a phyllodes tumor, the next step is grading, and grading is very important because it predicts and correlates with biological behavior and also how to, in terms of management, surgical procedures. So it's actually graded as benign, borderline, and malignant based on six features. For benign phyllodes tumors, all five features must be present: a well-defined border; mild stromal cellularity; stromal atypia ranging from none to mild; mitotic activity of less than five per 10 high-power fields (HPF); and no stromal overgrowth or malignant heterologous elements. To diagnose a malignant phyllodes tumor, the WHO currently requires all five features, although recent studies suggest this may not always be necessary. However, currently, all five are needed: an infiltrative border; markedly increased stromal cellularity; marked stromal atypia; mitotic activity greater than 10 per 10 HPF; and stromal overgrowth, often diffuse. The presence of malignant heterologous elements, even without all five other features, automatically classifies the tumor as malignant. Malignant heterologous elements exclude low-grade liposarcoma-like differentiation. Borderline phyllodes tumors exhibit some but not all features of malignant phyllodes tumors and lack malignant heterologous elements.

segments.transcript: So, because we know that phyllodes tumors can have a local recurrence, and malignant ones have metastatic potential, surgical excision is the goal. Breast conservation is preferred if feasible. Historically, a 1 cm margin of normal tissue was suggested, but this was arbitrary. More recent meta-analyses failed to identify a correlation between margin width and local recurrence, particularly in benign and lower-end borderline phyllodes tumors. These tumors have a low recurrence risk that may be independent of margin status. The 2024 NCCN guidelines suggest complete mass removal (excisional biopsy) without the intent of achieving negative margins; clinical follow-up for 3 years is recommended. Borderline or malignant phyllodes tumors require wide excision; however, the minimum margin width for borderline and malignant tumors is uncertain. An expert panel has suggested <1 mm as a positive margin. NCCN 2024 still suggests ≥1 cm but notes that lesser margin widths are not an absolute indication for mastectomy. Axillary lymph node staging is not indicated if there are no clinically suspicious lymph nodes. Currently, there is no routine role for radiation or chemotherapy unless the patient has a recurring tumor or a very large tumor that cannot be operated on; in such cases, chemotherapy may be given first to reduce tumor size.

segments.transcript: Patients with BRCA1/2 mutations and other hereditary breast/ovarian carcinomas have an increased lifetime risk for both breast and gynecological tumors. These tumors often share ER+ and PR+ immunophenotypes, which is not helpful in distinguishing them. However, breast markers such as mammoglobin, GZFP, GATA3, SOX10, PAX8, and WT1 can aid in differentiating primary tumor sites. WT1 (nuclear) is positive in ovarian serous carcinomas; mucinous carcinomas of the breast may also be positive. PAX8 (nuclear) is positive in most gynecological non-mucinous epithelial tumors, as well as in kidney and thyroid tumors. A subset of triple-negative breast carcinomas may also be PAX8 positive. CA125 (cytoplasmic) has low specificity. This slide presents additional markers for metastatic workup, differentiating breast cancer from other organ systems. For distinguishing breast cancer from lung cancer, TTF-1, Napsin-A, and SOX10 are helpful markers; however, small cell carcinoma may show TTF-1 positivity, and ER+ can be present in lung adenocarcinoma. To differentiate breast cancer from ovarian cancer, WT-1 and PAX8 are useful, but consider that ER+/PR+ may be present in ovarian cancers and WT-1+/PAX8+ in some breast carcinomas. For breast versus liver, markers include Heppar1, arginase, and MOC31, although Heppar1+ can also be found in breast cancer. Finally, when distinguishing breast cancer from mesothelioma, Calretinin, WT-1, and CK5/6 are useful, with basal-like breast cancer presenting CK5/6+ and GATA3+ found in mesothelioma. Invasive micropapillary carcinoma can be present in multiple organ sites: breast, ovary, bladder, and lung. What is micropapillary? These are tumor nests which are surrounded by clear spaces. They tend to have aggressive behavior, in the sense that they have a higher risk of lymphovascular invasion (LVI) and lymph node metastasis. Therefore, it is important to recognize this morphology. Type B is more cellular, with solid nests or anastomosing sheets, and may show neuroendocrine differentiation. Importantly, these classifications have no prognostic significance; they are of diagnostic and histogenetic interest only. The image shows Type A on the left. Type A and Type B are two types of mucinous carcinoma. Type B shows a more solid growth pattern than Type A. And then, as I said, a chromogranin stain, type B, can have neuroendocrine differentiation, as seen in this example. They have a very good prognosis. Mucinous carcinoma has a favorable prognosis. Prognosis correlates with conventional prognostic factors such as grade, size, lymphovascular invasion (LVI), and lymph node (LN) status. Mucinous carcinoma should be reserved for those with a simple breast resection (SBR) grade 1 and 2. Invasive breast cancer (IBC) with mucinous features is used for grade 3 tumors. The majority of cases are luminal A type. All tumors should be typed and graded because grading provides additional prognostic information, even within special-type cancers. For example, lobular carcinoma grade 1 has a 10-year survival rate of 71%, while mucinous carcinomas grade 1 have an 86% survival rate. Lobular carcinoma grade 2 has a 55% survival rate, and grade 3 has a 38% survival rate. Mucinous carcinoma grade 2 has a 75% survival rate. This demonstrates that tumor type and grade significantly impact prognosis. Invasive micropapillary carcinoma is composed of micropapillae or small clusters of neoplastic cells floating within clear stromal spaces resembling lymphatic channels. It is rare as a pure cancer (1–2%) but more common as a mixed carcinoma (7%). Why is it important to recognize this? Because it is highly aggressive, tends to have a high incidence of lymph node metastasis and lymphovascular invasion, and presents at an advanced stage. Invasive ductal carcinoma (IDC) with focal micropapillary features shows a similarly poor prognosis.

segments.transcript: Okay. So, David Page was the first to define atypical lobular hyperplasia (ALH). These cells are similar to those seen in lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS), but involve less space. ALH is defined by less than 50% of the acini in the terminal duct lobular unit (TDLU) being expanded. When more than 50% of the acini within the TDLU are expanded, it is called LCIS. What does 'expanded' mean? There are two approaches. Some pathologists use the one proposed by David Page, which means the diameter of the acinus must be eight cells or more across. So, when at least 50% of the acini within the TDLU are eight cells or more across, it is called LCIS. Some pathologists use the caliber of the involved acini and compare it to adjacent normal lobules. If it is larger, then it is called expanded, but this is more variable since acini can be small or large. I prefer to use David Page's approach. The reason to distinguish ALH from LCIS is because there is a different risk. ALH has about a five-fold increased risk for future invasive cancer development, while LCIS has about a ten-fold increase. So, it is important to separate them using established criteria because this indicates a different future risk.

segments.transcript: Florid LCIS (FLCIS) shows type A or type B cells; it does not exhibit hybrid cytology. However, it is characterized by marked distension of the terminal duct lobular units (TDLUs) or ducts, resulting in a mass-forming appearance. When involving TDLUs, there is minimal stroma between the acini. This mass-forming LCIS is sometimes called florid LCIS. Alternatively, the spaces may be markedly expanded, occupying at least one high-powered field (40-50 cells in diameter). Similar to cribriform LCIS, florid LCIS can be associated with comedonecrosis and calcifications. segments.transcript: What are the differences of pyromorphic and florid LCIS? This is because they show different biomarker profiles. Classic LCIS is always ER positive and HER2 negative, and they have low Ki67. Florid LCIS does not have high-grade cytology; they are typically ER positive, HER2 negative, although some cases may be positive (a very small percentage), but they actually have a higher Ki67. It is probably understandable why they can grow in significantly extended ducts. Most importantly, pleomorphic LCIS is more likely to be ER positive, and some will be HER2 positive, and some can even be triple negative. In addition, they also have a higher Ki67 and may show TP53 mutation, which is not seen in classic or florid LCIS. This shows an example of pleomorphic LCIS negative for ER, positive for HER2, and fairly high Ki67. We analyzed pyromorphologic LCIS and florid LCIS in a patient with classic LCIS, florid pyromorphologic LCIS, and invasive pyromorphologic LCIS. We dissected these individual lesions and analyzed them by next-generation sequencing. Classic LCIS showed very little change, only a 16q loss as expected. However, pyromorphologic LCIS showed many more chromosomal changes and genetic mutations, similar to pyromorphologic-associated invasive lobular carcinoma (ILC). These are genetically more advanced and similar to invasive lobular carcinoma.

segments.transcript: In 1941, Foote and Stewart made a significant observation regarding Lobular Carcinoma In Situ (LCIS). Eighty years ago, before immunostaining, they described many clinical and pathological features of LCIS that we now know. They noted that LCIS is clinically inconspicuous and not detectable by clinical examination or imaging. Even growth evaluation fails to reveal it. They also described classic morphological features: lesions involving the terminal duct lobular unit (TDLU), uniform cells with loss of cohesion and polarity, very rare mitoses, no necrosis, and pagetoid growth to larger ducts. Interestingly, they associated these lesions with a distinctive type of invasive carcinoma—infiltrating small cell carcinoma, now known as invasive lobular carcinoma.

segments.transcript: Lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS) was first described by Dr. C.D. Haagensen in 1978. Many studies were conducted, observing that some patients did not undergo a procedure even when a mastectomy was recommended. These studies found that LCIS is more of a risk factor for invasive breast cancer than a true precursor, as many patients with LCIS do not develop invasive breast cancer. However, they have an 8 to 10 times increased risk compared to the general population. Interestingly, when invasive breast cancer does develop, it can be bilateral and is more often invasive ductal carcinoma (IDC) than invasive lobular carcinoma (ILC). Because of the bilaterality and the higher incidence of IDC, LCIS is considered a risk factor rather than a precursor. To avoid overtreatment associated with the term LCIS, Dr. Haagensen, a breast surgeon and pathologist, proposed the term 'lobular neoplasia,' which later included both LCIS and atypical lobular hyperplasia (ALH).

segments.transcript: That's a brief history. Now, let's discuss classic lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS) and atypical lobular hyperplasia (ALH). LCIS and ALH show no clinical or growth abnormalities and are often incidental microscopic findings from breast biopsies or excisions performed for other reasons. However, they can be associated with cancer and are potential targets, though this represents a small portion of cases. The incidence is difficult to determine due to incidental findings, but based on breast biopsies, the incidence of LCIS among invasive cancers is approximately 0.4% to 3.6%. Looking at reduction mammoplasty specimens, the incidence ranges from less than 1% to 1.2%. The majority of patients are perimenopausal, with a mean age of 50 years old. It's a multifocal disease in up to 80% of patients, with multiple foci of LCIS in the same breast. Depending on the series, 13% to 60% present with bilateral disease. LCIS diagnosis is similar to that of Dr. Lee-Jin's method. One should examine the architecture and cytology. Architecturally, it typically involves lobules, sometimes spreading in a pagetoid manner. It presents in a solid pattern, lacking the cribriform or micropapillary patterns seen in other lesions. The characteristic feature is a loss of cell-to-cell cohesion due to dysfunctional E-cadherin. Cytologically, LCIS is composed of round or polygonal cells with uniform, round nuclei and homogeneous chromatin. Intracytoplasmic clear (mucin-filled) vacuoles (luminal) may be present, creating signet ring cells. A targetoid, dot-like material may be visible in vacuoles (lumina). Minimal atypia, rare mitoses, and no necrosis are typical.

segments.transcript: Initially, when discussing LCIS, especially in proximity to invasive lobular carcinoma, it was considered a precursor lesion. However, other studies suggest LCIS is more accurately characterized by its risk factors. The long-term risk for invasive cancer is significant, as it takes time to develop. When cancer does develop in patients with LCIS, it can be bilateral and present as invasive ductal carcinoma (IDC) or invasive lobular carcinoma (ILC), with IDC being more common. Nevertheless, LCIS remains a precursor lesion; patients with LCIS are three times more likely to develop ILC than the general population. Even with bilateral presentation, ipsilateral tumors tend to be lobular, further suggesting a precursor role. Genetic studies have demonstrated a relationship between LCIS and adjacent ILC, confirmed through techniques like comparative genomic hybridization (CGH) and next-generation sequencing, which reveal shared genetic alterations. Therefore, LCIS acts as both a risk factor and a precursor lesion, but a non-obligate one.

Several small studies, however, show limitations due to the slow progression of the disease and the need for large, long-term patient series for accurate risk assessment. Even with these limitations, the risk of developing invasive cancer is estimated to be around 1% per year for women with LCIS, even without intervention. Managing classic lobular neoplasia detected on core needle biopsy is controversial. Studies on patients with LCIS on core needle biopsy show a wide range (0–33%) in the percentage of those who subsequently develop cancer. This variation is due to factors like the lack of radiologic-pathologic correlation in some studies and the involvement of additional lesions in others. Studies with higher upgrade percentages usually lack radiologic-pathologic correlation.

segments.transcript: The management of classic lobular neoplasia on core needle biopsy (CNB), when identified and without biopsy, requires careful radiologic-pathologic correlation. These cases usually go to a radiologic-pathologic correlation conference or tumor board. After correlation, if LCIS and AOG are considered incidental findings and show a low upgrade rate, excision can be spared. These patients require active surveillance, but because approximately 1% may develop invasive cancer yearly, some patients may prefer risk reduction. One option is to offer risk reduction with anti-estrogen therapy. If radiologic-pathologic correlation reveals discordance or other lesions requiring excision, such as ADH, excision is recommended. Many of these patients will upgrade to invasive cancer. If there is discordance between the imaging and the pathology findings, then excision to explore for invasive cancer and DCIS is necessary.

Recent NCCN guidelines recommend that if classic LCIS shows concordant findings, the patient does not need immediate excision and can be offered risk reduction measures. However, if imaging is non-concordant, a surgical procedure is recommended. We know how to handle Lobular Carcinoma In Situ (LCS) in core biopsies, but what about when we see it in excisions? LCS is a multifocal disease, so even if the patient tests negative, there may still be residual LCS. Given that it's a non-obligate precursor, when LCS is present in an excision, the doctor doesn't need to evaluate the margins like we would for Ductal Carcinoma In Situ (DCIS), and the surgeon won't re-excise the LCS even if it's at the margin. Let's quickly discuss differential diagnosis. LCS has characteristic architecture and cytological features, making diagnosis usually easy; however, overdiagnosis and underdiagnosis are potential problems. Overdiagnosis can occur due to poor fixation, clear cell change, or prominent myoepithelial cells. Underdiagnosis is possible with subtle ALH or ductal involvement, especially in post-menopausal women.

segments.transcript: It is important to separate classic LCIS from DCIS because their biology is different. DCIS is considered a more direct precursor of invasive cancer, while classic LCIS is a risk factor for future invasive cancers, although it is a non-obligate precursor. DCIS has a continuous, segmental distribution, whereas LCIS is discontinuous and multifocal. The treatment for DCIS is surgical excision, often followed by radiation therapy (XRT) and/or hormonal therapy. Treatment for LCIS involves lifelong follow-up and may include hormonal therapy. Margins are not evaluated on excision for LCIS, but they are reported and require surgical clearance for DCIS. In core needle biopsy (CNB), active surveillance is used for LCIS if concordant with imaging, while excision is necessary for DCIS.

segments.transcript: E-cadherin is important in daily practice and is usually easy to interpret. However, there are pitfalls. Approximately 15% of lobular carcinomas show E-cadherin staining due to mutations leading to abnormal protein synthesis. Aberrant staining patterns include dot-like or Golgi, granular or cytoplasmic, fragmented/partial membranous, and circumferential but weak membranous staining. An impaired E-cadherin/catenin complex can also result in abnormal staining with other catenins. Weak membrane staining can be difficult to interpret, as even normal cells may resemble lobular carcinoma; in these situations, additional tests may be helpful to confirm the diagnosis of lobular lesions. For instance, this was actually an intraductal lesion, and the pathologist sent it to us because they thought that this was LCIS. However, when they did the E-cadherin stain, it showed positive staining. So there is this lobular appearance, but if you look more carefully, this is really a psychopathic granular staining. So this is actually considered aberrant staining. So even though it's positive staining, it's not the membrane staining; this actually supports this as a lobular carcinoma in situ. This slide shows another example of LCIS. You can see some membrane, but the abnormal staining pattern is granular and hyposomic. The staining is intense, almost like that seen in a Golgi apparatus. This apparent staining supports the diagnosis of LCIS.

segments.transcript: Based on this study, we know there are differences between classic LCIS and pleomorphic/florid LCIS (PLCIS/FLCIS), despite similar e-cadherin expression. First, PLCIS/FLCIS patients are approximately 10 years older. PLCIS/FLCIS are often detected mammographically (often as calcifications) due to necrosis, calcification, or architectural distortion; they are not clinically silent, as evidenced by non-mass enhancement on MRI. PLCIS/FLCIS exhibit more aggressive biomarkers and genetic changes. Genetically, they share the 1q gain and 16q loss characteristic of lobular neoplasia, linking them to carcinomas rather than ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS). However, they possess additional changes. Carcinomas show CDH1 and PIK3CA mutations, with few others, while PLCIS/FLCIS, particularly pleomorphic lobular carcinoma in situ, demonstrate more mutations, including TP53, ERBB2 (HER2), ERBB3, and CCND1. Though HER2 isn't amplified, mutations can lead to sensitivity to HER2-targeted therapies. Invasive lobular carcinomas with ERBB2 mutations may also show CCND1 and PIK3CA mutations. Classic LCIS has a very low incidence of adjacent invasive lobular carcinoma (ILC) or invasive ductal carcinoma (IDC), which is why complete excision isn't always necessary. Pure PLCIS/FLCIS is rare; when present in core biopsies without invasive cancer, 30-40% of excised cases reveal invasive cancer, mostly ILC. In contrast, with classic LCIS, adjacent invasive cancer (IDC or ILC) is less frequent.

These lesions are relatively recently recognized, so we have no long-term clinical follow-up data; their natural history is largely unknown. However, they have more aggressive biomarker profiles than classic LCIS and more genetic changes. Many are identical to associated invasive lobular carcinoma. They also have a high incidence of adjacent invasive cancer; some studies show almost 100% being invasive lobular carcinoma (ILC). These LCIS variants are genetically and likely biologically more advanced than classic LCIS, and are likely direct precursor lesions to invasive lobular cancer. segments.transcript: This slide shows the evolution of lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS) from 1941 to 2019. In 1941, classic LCIS was first recognized. Later, atypical lobular hyperplasia (ALH) and florid LCIS were identified. Studies showed that CLCIS has an 8 to 10 times higher risk of invasive cancer. Further research indicated that pleomorphic LCIS is an in situ lesion with pleomorphic ILC and pleomorphic nuclei. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) and array comparative genomic hybridization (aCGH) studies revealed that PLCIS/FLCIS has a more aggressive biomarker profile than CLCIS. Finally, next-generation sequencing (NGS) studies confirmed a clonal relationship with stepwise progression from CLCIS to PLCIS/FLCIS to invasive lobular carcinoma (ILC), showing that PLCIS/FLCIS is genetically and biologically more advanced than CLCIS. The most recent AJCC guidelines remove LCIS as a pTis category. LCIS is now treated as a benign entity and removed from the TNM staging. Regarding pleomorphic LCIS, evidence is insufficient at present, primarily due to the low prevalence of this form of high-grade LCIS, to establish definitive recommendations. Thus, for the present, high-grade or pleomorphic LCIS is also not included in the pTis classification.

The epithelium can be benign, called a papilloma, or malignant, called papillary carcinoma. As a reminder, the difference between micropapillary and papillary patterns is that they both have frond-like structures; however, the micropapillary pattern lacks a fibrovascular core, which is present in the papillary pattern. segments.transcript: The distinction between atypical ductal hyperplasia (ADH) and low-grade ductal carcinoma in situ (LG DCIS) can be problematic. ADH often coexists with LG DCIS, especially at the periphery of the DCIS. In 20–30% of patients with ADH on core needle biopsy (CNB), the diagnosis is upgraded to carcinoma (DCIS or invasive carcinoma) in excision. Therefore, careful distinction is crucial for appropriate patient management. The Society of Breast Surgeons recommends surgical excision as the standard of care for atypical ductal hyperplasia (ADH) diagnosed on core biopsy. However, there is an exception for very small volumes of ADH, such as one or two ducts, associated with calcification. In such cases, if radiology confirms that all calcifications have been removed, excision may not be necessary, and observation could be considered. These cases, however, require discussion within a multidisciplinary tumor board and close follow-up. The standard of management for ADH on core biopsy remains surgical excision. How about ALH and the classic LCIS on the cobalt? So, whether we need to excise classic lesions is the question.

segments.transcript: It is important to avoid overdiagnosis of low-grade DCIS on core biopsy. Many breast pathologists do not call a 2–3 millimeter area of pure low-grade DCIS as such, because some patients may opt for a mastectomy due to family history or prior diagnoses of low-grade or intermediate-grade DCIS that were completely excised. Overdiagnosis of small low-grade DCIS leads to unnecessary labeling of the patient. Instead of labeling small low-grade DCIS, it is better to communicate that it is a borderline feature, for example, by using terms such as 'severe ADH,' 'marked ADH,' 'atypical intraductal proliferation,' or 'ADH bordering on DCIS.' A conservative approach is to defer final classification to excision if necessary to avoid unnecessary procedures.

segments.transcript: Lobular neoplasia on core biopsy is controversial in recent years. It is a confirmed multi-sensory bilateral cancer, which can be invasive ductal or invasive lobular. Lobular neoplasia is considered a class of LCIS and ALH, acting as a marker for increased breast cancer risk in both breasts, although it can be a precursor and take a long time to progress. The upgrade rate is highly variable, with most recent studies showing approximately a 5% rate for classic LCIS and ALH. Importantly, good radiopathologic correlation exists, with low discordance. This study shows that with good radiologic-pathologic correlation in breast core biopsies, the upgrade rate is low, and the resulting cancers tend to be low-grade. However, with poor correlation, there is a much higher upgrade rate; in this study, it was 40%. This study examined the incidence of adjacent synchronous invasive carcinoma and/or ductal carcinoma in situ in patients with lobular neoplasia on core biopsy. ALH or classic LCIS was identified as the highest-risk lesion. Concordant radiologic-pathologic findings were observed, and a central pathology review was conducted. The upgrade rate was 3% by local pathology and 1% by central pathology review. Of 79 core needle biopsies (CNBs), 77 excisions were performed. Seventy-five lesions showed concordant findings, with 74 (99%) not upgraded and 1 (1%) upgraded to invasive ductal carcinoma in situ (IG DCIS). Two disagreements in diagnosis were identified: one tubular carcinoma in CNB and one case with no lymph node involvement in CNB. The median time between CNB and excision was 2 months. This slide shows the upgrade rates of ALH/LCIS on core biopsy with radiologic-pathologic correlation. The data is presented in a table showing the number of core biopsies and excisions, as well as the number and percentage of carcinomas, DCIS, and invasive cancers for ALH and LCIS separately. The total upgrade rate is approximately 5%.

segments.transcript: Mucocele-like lesions were first described in 1986 by Rosen. He initially thought they were benign analogs to the mucus seals of minor salivary glands. A mucus-filled lesion is usually dark and resembles stromal mucus because the mucus-filled area ruptures. However, Rosen later published that not all mucoceles are benign because they represent a spectrum, with some epithelial lesions exhibiting features of atypical ductal hyperplasia (ADH) or ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS). Therefore, it's a spectrum. It occurs in a wide age range (24-79 years, mean ~50 years) and is rare, accounting for approximately 0.3% of core needle biopsies (CNB). The majority are due to mammographic abnormality; 80-90% present with calcifications, while the rest present as a mass lesion. When mucus is seen in a lesion, the presence of epithelial atypia should be evaluated. However, with exigencies, epithelial atypia can be focal and present on a spectrum, sometimes only accessible in certain areas. This is a concern when evaluating mucus in lesions due to the potential for focal and patchy involvement. Additionally, mucus lesions may contain epithelium within the stromal mucin. This does not automatically indicate mucinous carcinoma, as the epithelium could be detached from denuded ducts. A key challenge is distinguishing between displaced epithelium within mucus versus true mucinous carcinoma. Careful evaluation is needed.

segments.transcript: We know there are many challenges in the diagnosis of lung cancer. As a pathology site, we are asked for comprehensive and complex diagnostics using minimally invasive procedures. Of course, we must integrate these diagnostics within the world of personalized therapy. So, the integration of biomarkers in the clinical management of the cancer patient is a necessity. Importantly, many patients, more than 50-60% of those with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), present for the first time at advanced stages. For these patients, what we often have is only cytological material and/or small biopsies for both diagnosis and biomarker studies. At the same time, there is a development of emerging techniques that allow for non-invasive approaches, from which we obtain the same type of samples: cytological material and/or small biopsies. Therefore, without any doubt, fine needle aspiration (FNA/FNAC) and fine needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB) are in the first line, not only in the diagnosis but also in the overall management of a patient with non-small cell lung cancer.

segments.transcript: One methodology used with increasing frequency in different hospitals is the Endobronchial Ultrasound (EBUS) guided FNA. It is an FNA performed through the bronchoscope, using real-time ultrasound guidance. This allows us to sample not only central lung lesions, but also mediastinal and peribronchial lymph nodes. When we use invasive methodology, such as trans-thoracic FNA, it's advisable to have a Rapid On-Site Evaluation (ROSE). Because during ROSE, we can not only tell the clinician, 'Okay, I have material,' but also split the material for the different ancillary techniques that I will eventually need, according to the type of pathology I'm looking for. For example, if I'm looking for non-small cell lung cancer in a lung, I know that I will probably need immunohistochemistry and molecular testing. If I'm looking at lymphoid proliferation, I will probably need flow cytometry. And during ROSE, I can separate this material according to the further studies that might be needed. Knowing our role in lung pathology, let's move to the reporting system. We know that there are many advantages to using a standardized terminology in pathology. This standardized terminology unifies reporting of disease categories, providing well-defined diagnostic criteria and a well-defined risk of malignancy. It reduces interobserver variability, improves intra-observer reproducibility, better aligns patient management options with interpretations, and ultimately improves patient care.

We tested various markers, and while some showed good correlation, for others, such as surface lambda, the correlation between the two methods was not optimal. When we looked for light-chain restriction, we found that with two-color flow cytometry, restriction was identified in 70% of cases, indicative of lymphoma, whereas with immunocytochemistry, it was only identified in 45% of cases. We therefore concluded that the flow cytometric method is more sensitive and specific than the immunocytochemical method, which led us to purchase our first two-color flow cytometer. The year 1997 is therefore considered as the beginning of... Flow cytometry, flow cytometric immunotyping, and modern cytopathological diagnostics of lymphoma at our hospital. At the beginning, we had a lot of problems. First of all, more than half of cytological samples had too few cells to perform flow cytometric measurements. We also had problems with the interpretation of the results. We didn't know what it meant when the surface immunoglobulins were negative. What to do with cases where we observed one or two populations of CD3 positive cells? And the problem was also that the sensitivity of lymphoma detection at the beginning was unsatisfactory.

segments.transcript: Finally, I'm just going to finish on what are the usual features of lymph node fine needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB) cytopathology. Well, they usually show high cellularity if the smear is well-done and well-made, and usually a highly dispersed cell pattern, which helps us confirm we're dealing with a lymphoid population and not something else like metastatic cancer. And of course, we see fragments of lymphoid cell cytoplasm, or as they're commonly known, lymphoglandular bodies. I'm going to suggest there are eight lymphoid patterns for reactive and lymphomatous lymph nodes, often with lymphoid tissue fragments. These can be hard to see unless you're dealing with well-made material. However, there's often a germinal center tissue fragment in a dispersed pattern. We typically see a small to intermediate lymphoid cell pattern with small lymphocytes predominating. So, these are the hallmarks for follicular hyperplasia. You can also have follicular nodules, again, with a dispersed mixed population of small to intermediate lymphoid cells, including centrocytes and centroblasts, but importantly, not small lymphocytes predominating. The classic example here is follicular lymphoma. When tissue fragments are absent, lymphoid patterns can be categorized. One pattern is a resting or quiescent, sometimes reactive lymph node, characterized by predominantly small lymphocytes in a dispersed population. Another pattern is a mixed population of small and intermediate lymphoid cells, with small lymphocytes predominating, plus prominent immunoblasts. This represents the classic immunoblastic reaction, often seen in viral infections. Finally, a dispersed mixed population of small and intermediate lymphoid cells, with small lymphocytes predominating, but also featuring very large numbers of histiocytes, is prototypically seen in Rosai-Dorfman disease or sinus histiocytosis.

This appearance is considered a senescence phenomenon, a degenerative type of endocrine atypia. Histologically, these tumors are often nested, resembling paragangliomas. It's crucial not to misdiagnose them as paragangliomas, especially if a keratin stain is not performed, as it would be positive in a neuroendocrine tumor and negative in paragangliomas. The key point for daily practice regarding atypical glandular cells is: If atypical glandular cells are present and one cannot determine if they are neoplastic or reactive, the best diagnosis is: “Atypical cells present.” Add a comment to correlate clinically and radiologically, and consider repeating the FNA. My observation is that when there's a high suspicion of malignancy, a repeat FNA will be diagnostic for malignancy in about 60% of cases.

segments.transcript: So the undifferentiated carcinoma with osteoclast-like giant cells, some people call it osteoclastic giant cell carcinoma, is a very rare form of pancreatic cancer. These often have an adenocarcinoma component, which can be variable in amount; it can be very small and focal, or it can be the predominant component, but usually there is an adenocarcinoma component in almost half of these cases. These tumors interestingly have a better prognosis than conventional PDAC, but in our recent study where we looked at 15 of these cases on cytology, we found that for patients who actually had an FNA done on these tumors, this good prognosis did not seem, it was not the case after FNA was performed. Now whether this poor prognosis was linked to the actual FNA itself or was just a coincidence, we cannot be sure, but this was just an interesting observation we found. There are three characteristic cell types that you see. In this subtype, there are three distinct cell types. First, benign osteoclastic giant cells (OGCs) are multinucleated histocytes expressing histocytic markers. They are completely benign, lack mutations, and are negative for keratin. Unlike OGCs, there are two types of malignant tumor cells. Malignant tumor giant cells are large, pleomorphic, with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic (N/C) ratio, often showing K-RAS mutations. They are positive for keratin and negative for histocytic markers. The other malignant cell type is spindled or histocytoid cells, which are smaller, rounder, and less pleomorphic than tumor giant cells. These spindled cells exhibit variable expression of both histocytic markers and keratin.

A cell under stress physiologically doubles the whole genome to be more effective, and that doubles all the chromosomes. So, if you have two copies for each chromosome in normal cells, you have four copies for each chromosome in tetraploid cells. It doesn't mean that it's a tumor cell, because it can also occur in reactive conditions. That's a potential pitfall in this assay: if you call tetraploid cells as positive, then you may create false positive cases.

segments.transcript: Another important aspect of FISH testing in urinary cytology is that you want to look at specific cells or cell groups of interest, and not just take a specimen and go randomly over it. It's much more rewarding with automatic relocation using an automated stage. First, you relocate your cells, identify and save the coordinates of the cells, process the sample for FISH, and then go back to those very same cells. This way, you really know what you want to know and limit the possibility of looking at the wrong cells. This facilitates review and sign-out time. segments.transcript: Urinary cytology is not new, having been described 77 years ago as a useful tool to potentially detect neoplastic cells in urine. This discovery was made by George Papanicolaou, who published his findings in a very prestigious journal. Much has happened since then. The indications for urinary cytology as we do it is usually hematuria (voided urine). If a person has hematuria, cytology of the urine is the first thing that is usually being done. A significant proportion of cytology specimens that are seen in a, let's say, academic environment are for surveillance. And the other side of the cytology is in patients who had earlier resected urothelial cancer, knowing that these tumors recur in usually 70% of all cases. Another intriguing indication is control of therapy with intravesical BCG to see whether it was successful or not. And we have known for a long time that detection of CIS and non-visible high-grade cancer is the main purpose and the main strength of urinary cytology. Now, looking at the types of urinary cytology that we encounter. The proportions vary depending on where you work. In some environments, it's voided urine. Now, in many environments, it's mostly bladder washing. And then, catheter urine is less common. Upper urinary tract cytology, brushes, or washings, but also forced diuresis after giving diuretics is also a typical indication. And there are others, less common ones, which I won't get into.

segments.transcript: Low-grade urothelial neoplasia (LGUN) was a category in the TPS1 system, but it is no longer a distinct category in TPS2. It has been incorporated into the 'Negative for High-Grade Urothelial Carcinoma (NHGUC)' category. This is because LGUN is by definition negative for high-grade features, a point everyone agrees on. Nevertheless, we can still make a descriptive diagnosis of LGUN in the text if a case clearly demonstrates these features, but its official TPS category will be 'Negative for High-Grade'. This change emphasizes the importance of distinguishing between 'Negative for High-Grade' and 'High-Grade Urothelial Carcinoma', rather than spending too much time dissecting the diagnosis of LGUN. To make a descriptive diagnosis of LGUN, you need to identify true papillae, which are cellular three-dimensional clusters with a fibrovascular core. If a fibrovascular core is absent, you cannot definitively diagnose LGUN, but you can suspect it if other features are present. These include cellular clusters, numerous monotonous single cells (not umbrella cells) with uniform cytoplasm, mild irregularities of the nuclear membrane, and an increased N/C ratio. Regardless of suspicion, such cases always fall under the 'Negative for High-Grade' category. For example, in cytology, if you observe a highly cellular papillary structure with monotonous cells and an increased N/C ratio, but no features of high-grade urothelial carcinoma, this represents LGUN and is categorized as 'Negative for High-Grade Urothelial Carcinoma'.

segments.transcript: Whenever there is necrosis, you may observe varying degrees of regeneration as the liver attempts to heal. When the liver tries to regenerate, it forms circular arrangements of hepatocytes around dilated, liquefied canaliculi. These are referred to as rosettes and may sometimes contain bile plugs. Rosettes are generally seen in acute liver injury when the liver is trying to regenerate. While descriptions of rosettes are common in autoimmune hepatitis, they can also be observed in other forms of acute liver injury. The examples shown illustrate acute hepatitis, characterized by inflammation. Acute hepatitis involves varying degrees of hepatocellular injury with necrosis. This is what is referred to as an inflammation-dominant pattern of acute hepatitis. Once you see this pattern, there are a very limited number of etiologies that can lead to this, including acute viral hepatitis, adverse drug reactions, autoimmune hepatitis, or Wilson's disease. These are the most common differential diagnoses with this pattern of injury. You can also get acute hepatitis with a slightly different pattern of injury, in which there is not much inflammation, but the dominant finding is the presence of necrosis. The reason for necrosis without inflammation in this pattern is because the agents causing it are directly hepatotoxic; they do not require inflammation to cause injury, as opposed to etiologies where damage is mediated by inflammatory cells. This list of directly hepatotoxic causes includes toxins, drugs (like acetaminophen), non-hepatotropic viruses that characteristically lead to necrosis with very little inflammation, and vascular diseases. For instance, acetaminophen toxicity is an example of this necrosis-dominant pattern.

They exhibit serrated gland contours, with architectural complexity greater on the mucosal surface than in the deep part, distinguishing them from sessile serrated adenomas. The cytoplasm can be eosinophilic or mucinous, and the nuclei are round, non-dysplastic, difficult to see, and sit basally in the cell without stratification. If you've gone on any general surgical pathology or gastrointestinal pathology sign-outs, you've certainly seen many of these polyps. People talk about the starfish profile when you cut these in cross-section. Keep in mind, however, that a sessile serrated adenoma also looks like a starfish on cross-section, but it has greater complexity throughout the full thickness of the mucosa. When we see these in longitudinal section, the serrations are visible.

segments.transcript: FAP is an inherited syndrome where individuals have a mutation in the APC gene, which is the basic driver of tubular adenomas. This is not a very common alteration, found in about 0.1% of the population worldwide, but it has a very impressive clinical presentation and incredible consequences. Individuals with classic FAP have more than 100 adenomatous polyps in the colon and essentially a 100% lifetime risk of cancer at a very young age. Even though only 0.1% of the population has this, it makes up about 1% of all colorectal cancer due to its high penetrance. Some individuals have attenuated familial adenomatous polyposis, with fewer than 100 polyps. The underlying defect here may still be an APC gene mutation, but one that is less damaging to the protein. For instance, a classic APC mutation might be a nonsense mutation causing the protein not to be made, whereas an attenuated FAP mutation might be a missense mutation where the protein is still made but with altered function. Alternatively, patients with attenuated FAP may have a mutation in a completely unrelated gene called MUTYH, which is involved in DNA repair. Because of this high lifetime risk of cancer, patients undergo prophylactic colectomy, usually in their 20s.

segments.transcript: Juvenile polyps often present with a 'Swiss cheese' appearance due to large cysts, which can be grossly visible. In some hereditary cases, a branched architecture may be present, mimicking a Peutz-Jeghers polyp. Hamartomatous polyps, including juvenile polyps, Peutz-Jeghers polyps, and those associated with PTEN deficiency (e.g., Cowden syndrome), frequently resemble inflammatory polyps histologically. This overlap means that while a polyp might be fundamentally juvenile, its histological appearance can be indistinguishable from an inflammatory polyp. Similar to hyperplastic polyps of the stomach, juvenile polyps typically feature an expanded lamina propria rich in inflammatory cells, though with less edema. Crypts often show significant cystic dilatation, visible even grossly. Furthermore, surface erosions and abundant granulation tissue contribute to their inflammatory polyp-like appearance. The baseline histology usually shows non-dysplastic nuclei, but secondary dysplasia can occur, particularly in syndromic cases.

It is associated with an increased risk of cancer, likely arising in a pre-existing polyp, as a significant number of polyps in patients with juvenile polyposis syndrome exhibit dysplasia. In contrast, dysplasia is rare in sporadic juvenile polyps. The underlying gene defects in juvenile polyposis are either SMAD4 (also known as DPC4) or Bone Morphogenic Protein Receptor 1A (BMPR1A); sporadic polyps do not typically have these same mutations. segments.transcript: Moving on to the Peutz-Jeghers polyp, which is more common in the small intestine. A key differentiating feature is its well-developed, thick, smooth muscle branches with arborizing architecture, unlike simple smooth muscle fibers. The baseline polyp has non-dysplastic nuclei, although secondary dysplasia can occur. Be aware of pseudoinvasion or misplaced epithelium, where epithelium appears invasive within the stalk but is associated with lamina propria and often lacks dysplastic features, distinguishing it from invasive carcinoma. Similar to juvenile polyps, it can exhibit surface injury, mimicking an inflammatory polyp. Dysplasia can be found in a small number of these polyps. The underlying mutation in both sporadic and syndromic polyps is STK11, also known as LKB1. While rare sporadic cases exist, most Peutz-Jeghers polyps are syndromic. This is a separate branch of this polyp. It is not one large polyp with smooth muscle throughout, which is characteristic of mucosal prolapse. Instead, there is a well-defined branch with a big, thick smooth muscle core, which is important for differentiating a Peutz-Jeghers polyp. On higher power, a well-developed fibromuscular core is visible.

segments.transcript: Moving on to eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE). This is considered an allergic disorder, more common in children but also seen in adults, with symptoms varying by patient age. For example, infants may have feeding difficulties, older children nausea and vomiting, and other patients dysphagia. An important diagnostic clue is that many patients have other allergic disorders, such as food allergy, asthma, eczema, chronic rhinitis, and environmental allergies. Also, on upper endoscopy, patients may demonstrate characteristic findings such as esophageal rings and longitudinal furrows. These changes are highly supportive of EoE. In severe situations, patients may present with esophageal narrowing that requires esophageal dilation. This is what an esophageal ring looks like, and there is longitudinal furrowing visible on endoscopy. These are some of the characteristic endoscopic findings in patients with EOE, and are considered defining features of EOE.

segments.transcript: Eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE) is characterized by a markedly increased intraepithelial eosinophil count, usually more than 15 eosinophils per one high-power field. It is a very diffuse process involving both the proximal and distal esophagus, unlike reflux esophagitis, which is typically limited to the distal esophagus. However, it's important to note that there is no minimum number of eosinophils required for diagnosis; for instance, if a patient is treated with steroids or dietary modification, the number of intraepithelial eosinophils may decrease over time. Additional histologic features can further support the diagnosis of EoE, such as eosinophilic microabscesses (defined as a cluster of four or more eosinophils), superficial layering of eosinophils in the upper one-third to one-half of the squamous epithelium, and eosinophilic degranulation. Like other types of esophagitis, EoE frequently presents with evidence of epithelial damage, including basal zone hyperplasia, elongation of papillae, and spongiosis. While severe cases of reflux esophagitis may also present with more than 15 intraepithelial eosinophils per high-power field, this is typically more limited to the distal esophagus without involving the proximal portion. Ultimately, the distinction from reflux esophagitis relies on clinicopathologic correlation, and it's important to remember that none of these clinical symptoms, endoscopic findings, or histologic features are specific for EoE. This is an example of eosinophilic esophagitis (EOE), showing more than 15 intraepithelial eosinophils per high-power field. There is also evidence of eosinophilic degradation present. This represents another example of EOE.

segments.transcript: The distal esophagus should show a marked increase in intraepithelial eosinophils, probably more than 15 eosinophils per high-power field. There is a superficial layering of eosinophils involving the upper one-third to one-half of the squamous epithelium. Also, there is some evidence of epithelial damage, with expansion of the basal zone exceeding 15% of the epithelial thickness. Furthermore, there is elongation of papillae, extending beyond two-thirds of the epithelial thickness. From the same patient, the esophagus biopsy essentially shows identical histologic features. There is a markedly increased intraepithelial eosinophil count, and eosinophil microabscesses are present, defined as a cluster of four or more eosinophils. Additionally, there is evidence of epithelial damage, basal zone hyperplasia, spongiosis, and elongation of papillae. In terms of treatment for EoE, some patients respond to dietary modification, including an elimination diet based on skin pre-testing. Some patients may require an elemental diet, which is done by replacing all solid food with a synthetic amino acid formula. Some patients respond by removing common foods associated with EoE, such as milk, egg, wheat, corn, soy, beef, or chicken. If patients do not respond to dietary modification, corticosteroids are required. For those patients who develop esophageal strictures, esophageal dilation is required in that setting.

segments.transcript: If an esophageal biopsy shows increased eosinophils, but less than 15 eosinophils per high-power field, involving only the distal portion of the esophagus with evidence of epithelial damage, basal cell hyperplasia, and elongation of papillae, the diagnosis is reflux esophagitis. If there are markedly increased intraepithelial eosinophils, more than 15 per high-power field, with a more diffuse process involving both proximal and distal esophagus, the diagnosis is Eosinophilic Esophagitis (EOE). If one observes more neutrophilic inflammation, often with ulcers, pseudohyphae, and spores, the diagnosis is Candida esophagitis. If multinucleated squamous cells are present with characteristic cytopathic changes, including nuclear molding, chromatin margination, and ground-glass intranuclear inclusions, the diagnosis is HSV esophagitis. If a very prominent intranuclear inclusion surrounded by a clear halo is seen, along with coarse intracytoplasmic granules, the diagnosis is CMV esophagitis. If a cluster of cocci and bacilli invading the esophageal wall and blood vessels with associated necrosis is identified, the diagnosis is bacterial esophagitis. Finally, if a polarizable fragment with an associated giant cell reaction is found, usually more common in the mid-esophagus where inflammatory narrowing occurs, the diagnosis is also bacterial esophagitis.

segments.transcript: Microscopically, HSV esophagitis presents with nuclear molding, chromatin margination, and ground-glass intranuclear inclusions. The background often shows neutrophilic inflammation mixed with other inflammatory cells like eosinophils and lymphocytes. Necrotic debris may also be present. While typically a self-limited condition in healthy populations, HSV esophagitis can potentially lead to complications such as esophageal perforation or disseminated disease, especially in immunocompromised patients. CMV esophagitis looks a little bit different from HSV esophagitis. It shows very distinct cytopathic changes. It also has large infected cells with a prominent intranuclear inclusion surrounded by a clear halo. It also shows coarse intracytoplasmic granules, as you can see here. Typically, I'm showing neutrophil infiltration with ulceration, but this particular example shows more predominantly lymphocyte infiltration.

segments.transcript: Starting with gastroesophageal reflux disease, also known as reflux esophagitis, this is a relatively common entity; approximately 20% of the population in the United States experiences some degree of reflux esophagitis. This condition is caused by the reflux of gastric content into the esophagus. Patients may present with varying symptoms, including heartburn, dysphagia, chest pain, and regurgitation. Most patients do not undergo an endoscopy unless they have severe symptoms, fail PPI therapy, or have some risk factors for esophagitis or adenocarcinoma. It is important to note that up to 50% of patients, even if they undergo an endoscopy, may show normal findings without any significant changes. However, some patients may have mild, non-specific changes such as mucosal erythema, edema, or erosion. In severe situations, ulceration and an inflammatory exudate may be observed, typically involving only the distal portion of the esophagus. At the moment, there is no completely sensitive or specific test for the diagnosis of reflux esophagitis.

segments.transcript: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is an inherited cancer syndrome. There is prominent mucocutaneous pigmentation in many individuals, which is how they are often diagnosed early on in life. There is a greatly increased risk of not only GI but also non-GI cancers, including breast cancers and testicular tumors. In the GYN tract, there are some very distinct tumors, such as sex cord tumor with annular tubules and a really well-differentiated cervical cancer called adenoma malignum. Patients face a greatly increased lifetime risk of cancer, making screening crucial. Patients with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome have an increased risk of GI cancers and undergo periodic small bowel imaging. The risk of cancer is not limited to polyps, as non-polyp mucosa can also develop cancer, indicating a generalized risk. The underlying defect is in the STK11/LKB1 gene, which is a serine/threonine kinase tumor suppressor. The same alteration is found in sporadic polyps, and this gene is also an important driver in lung cancer. If you think about the anatomy, the ampulla of Vater is the junction of the duodenum and the biliary system. At the ampulla, we have both types of epithelium: the duodenal mucosa and, right at the transition, the pancreatobiliary type mucosa of the duct. Each side of these can develop adenomas and carcinomas. When examining such tumors, one would probe along the ampulla to assess the type of epithelium involved, particularly if a tumor is arising from the intestinal tract. With the duodenal type of epithelium, one can observe something resembling a colonic tubular adenoma or an intestinal type adenoma. These adenomas can develop into an intestinal type adenocarcinoma.

segments.transcript: Duodenal biopsies are frequently performed for iron deficiency anemia (IDA) and suspected malabsorption, primarily because celiac disease is the etiology in 5-6% of IDA cases. They are also indicated in cases of peptic ulcer disease, inflammatory disorders such as Crohn's disease, and when there is concern for infection or tumor. Celiac disease is an immune-mediated disease related to a hypersensitivity to gluten. Celiac disease is an immune-mediated sensitivity to gluten, found in grains like barley, rye, and oats. There is a clear genetic predisposition, with most celiac patients having HLA class II DQ2, and some tending to have DQ8. However, it is not solely genetic, as most individuals with DQ2 do not develop celiac disease. Thus, having this HLA class does not guarantee celiac disease development. It is the number one cause of malabsorption, often diagnosed via duodenal biopsy, and is pretty common in the Western world, with an incidence of 1 in 200 to 1 in 300 people. The age of onset is variable and can be detected as early as childhood.
