segments.transcript: Celiac disease can manifest well into middle age and in elderly patients. Diagnosing it is clinically challenging because symptoms are highly variable and not specific, including malabsorption, diarrhea, steatorrhea, iron or folate deficiency, and irritable bowel syndrome-like symptoms. Since many of these complaints are common in primary care, biopsy is a crucial part of the diagnosis. Treating celiac disease is important not only due to the consequences of malabsorption but also to prevent serious long-term complications that can result from longstanding untreated disease, such as aggressive lymphoma (like EATL lymphoma) and the possibility of carcinoma. A key histopathological feature of celiac disease is villous atrophy. It's like someone took a lawn mower and just clipped off all of the villi. This occurs in more well-developed cases. Additionally, the crypts, which are typically short in the small intestine, become longer. If one were told this was a biopsy of the colon, it might be mistaken for such, as the crypts are much longer and the villi are absent. Thus, it basically creates a mimic of colonic mucosa in more well-developed cases. However, that is not the only change. Another key feature, present even in milder cases without these architectural changes, is an increase in intraepithelial lymphocytes. segments.transcript: This appears to be a well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor. On higher power, it shows nests of very uniform, very round cells with some pseudoglands. The neuroendocrine marker chromogranin is positive, which seals the deal that this is a well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor. A pseudoacinar pattern can mimic adenocarcinoma, but neuroendocrine markers help differentiate it. More proximal tumors are less likely to be associated with carcinoid syndrome. Here is an example of another type of tumor with pseudoacinar structures and sometimes psammoma bodies, which can also be seen in the jejunum and ileum. Well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumors arising in the jejunum/ileum are more likely to metastasize to the liver and develop carcinoid syndrome. Tumor behavior is predicted by size and local characteristics, and grading is based on mitotic activity and Ki-67. Carcinoid syndrome occurs in about five to seven percent of cases. Patients who have serotonin-secreting carcinoid tumors, typically arising in the distal small intestine, will experience symptoms when these tumors metastasize to the liver. This metastasis allows the tumor to dump serotonin directly into the bloodstream, leading to consequences of excess serotonin. Consequently, there are cardiac symptoms, such as fibrous thickening of the valves, due to the effect of serotonin on the heart and blood vessels.

segments.transcript: Peutz-Jeghers polyps, associated with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, are most common in the small bowel but can occur elsewhere. Their diagnosis is characterized by the presence of very complex arborizing smooth muscle and normal small intestinal epithelial cells. Due to their complex architecture and misplacement of epithelium, these polyps can mimic carcinoma, so it is important to look for features like desmoplasia before making a carcinoma diagnosis. Most Peutz-Jeghers polyps do not have dysplasia, but patients with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome have a greatly increased risk of carcinoma. While sporadic cases exist, most individuals with Peutz-Jeghers polyps likely have the syndrome, whether or not they have been diagnosed yet. The architecture features smooth muscle cores on the well-developed, very branching structures. This is a key diagnostic feature. Due to the complex architecture, one might initially consider invasive carcinoma; however, there is no desmoplasia, and the cells do not appear dysplastic. These architectural changes are likely due to the complex growth of these polyps. Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is an autosomal dominant condition.

Cryptosporidiosis is a common cause of diarrhea and biliary injury in AIDS patients, often manifesting as AIDS cholangiopathy. The organisms sit right on the surface of enterocytes. They are not within the cytoplasm, nor are they within the lamina propria. They simply sit along the surface of the epithelial cells. This micrograph illustrates a case of long-standing HIV enteropathy, showing another example of plentiful inflammatory cells. HIV/AIDS Enteropathy is a chronic infection, not due to celiac disease or peptic duodenitis. It is believed in most cases to be caused by chronic Cryptosporidium infection, but it is likely multifactorial, involving multiple infections causing chronic injury and architectural changes. This can affect the small intestine, causing changes similar to those seen in the colon. Another infectious organism is Microsporidia; unlike Cryptosporidia, these are actually present within the cytoplasm.

segments.transcript: H. pylori is the most common cause of chronic gastritis in many parts of the world, particularly in developing countries, infecting over 50% of the global population. Although the exact route of transmission is unknown, person-to-person transmission, likely oral-oral or fecal-oral, is suspected. H. pylori produces large amounts of urease, which breaks down urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide, causing a localized pH increase in its microenvironment. This mechanism allows the organism to survive in the hostile, acidic environment of the stomach. During the early part of the infection, H. pylori is predominantly found in the antrum, where the environment helps protect it from the acidity of the gastric content. Over time, inflammation progresses from the antrum to the body of the stomach, leading to the destruction and loss of parietal cells, mucosal atrophy, and a reduction in acid secretion. This can lead to the development of various types of epithelial metaplasia, such as intestinal metaplasia, and patients can potentially develop dysplasia and cancer later on. In patients on chronic PPI use, because H. pylori cannot survive at a pH of eight, it tends to migrate from the antrum to a more acidic environment of the oxyntic mucosa in the body or fundus of the stomach. Here, you will find the organism deep within the gland, sometimes inside the cells, as opposed to its usual superficial location. Therefore, in patients on chronic PPI use, you may need to order immunohistochemistry to look for H. pylori organisms hiding deep within the oxyntic gland. segments.transcript: Chronic and active gastritis are distinct. Chronic gastritis is characterized by a prominent lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate, often pushing aside the glands and presenting with lymphoid follicles with germinal centers. Active gastritis is defined by the presence of neutrophilic inflammation, involving the surface foveolar epithelium and/or glandular epithelium or crypts. After H. pylori eradication, while neutrophilic inflammation tends to disappear and epithelial damage heals within a few days, the chronic component regresses at a slower pace, especially in the long term. H. pylori can be easily identified on H&E without using any special stain or immunohistochemistry. H. pylori is a curved, S-shaped, or comma-shaped bacterium, very small in size, two to four microns in length. They are typically found on the surface and in the gastric pit lumens as a cluster of bacteria. Immunohistochemistry can be ordered to identify H. pylori organisms. This technique highlights these abundant bacterial organisms in brown. As previously mentioned, they are typically located on the gastric surface epithelium or within the gastric pit lumen as clusters of bacteria.

segments.transcript: This table compares and contrasts H. pylori gastritis and autoimmune gastritis. H. pylori gastritis is caused by H. pylori infection and affects all patients regardless of age or gender. Early in the infection, it is predominantly found in the antrum, but over time, H. pylori tends to migrate from the antrum to the body of the stomach, hiding deep within the oxyntic glands. Histologically, H. pylori gastritis demonstrates a predominant lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate, usually involving the superficial portion of the gastric mucosa, often with lymphoid follicles with germinal centers. Major complications include peptic ulceration, but patients may also develop adenocarcinoma (usually intestinal type) or extranodal marginal zone lymphoma. By contrast, autoimmune gastritis is an autoimmune disorder characterized by circulating autoantibodies targeting parietal cells and intrinsic factor. It predominantly affects middle-aged to elderly females and is limited to the body of the stomach. Histologically, it demonstrates a predominant lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate involving both superficial and deep portions of the gastric glands. Due to circulating autoantibodies and prominent lymphoplasmacytic cells, there is destruction of parietal cells. In return, there is a compensatory proliferation of G cells in the antrum, which secrete gastrin. This gastrin hormone causes neuroendocrine cells, including ECL cells, to proliferate in the body of the stomach. Consequently, these patients have a higher risk of developing neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia and multifocal neuroendocrine tumors. Autoimmune gastritis is also often associated with an increased risk of developing other autoimmune diseases.

segments.transcript: Moving on to collagenous gastritis, just like other forms of gastritis such as autoimmune gastritis, it typically demonstrates a prominent lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate involving the superficial portion of the gastric mucosa, as you can see here. This is characterized by a thickened subepithelial collagen band, often entrapping capillaries and inflammatory cells. There is also some evidence of epithelial damage, with flattening and detachment of the surface epithelium. The diagnosis can be confirmed using Trichrome stain, which highlights the thickened subepithelial collagen band with irregular branching into the lamina propria, as you can see here. Even though collagenous gastritis typically shows a primary lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate, some rare cases may present with an increased eosinophil count (more than 30 eosinophils per high-power field) or increased intraepithelial lymphocytes involving the surface and foveolar epithelium, potentially mimicking eosinophilic gastritis or lymphocytic gastritis, which will be discussed in a few minutes.

segments.transcript: There are two different types of collagenous gastritis: the adult form and the pediatric form. The adult form is more common in women, often associated with diffuse involvement of the GI tract, chronic watery diarrhea, and various autoimmune disorders. Even though its etiology is unclear, infection, autoimmune disease, and medication are regarded as possible triggers. Most adult patients have a chronic intermittent course without significant deterioration or mortality risk. By contrast, the pediatric form, even though sometimes limited to the stomach, typically presents with worse symptoms, including abdominal pain, bleeding, and anemia. Refractory cases with a poor response to steroid therapy are also more common in the pediatric population, and it can be potentially life-threatening. However, more recent data suggests a substantial overlap between the adult and pediatric forms, making distinction based on clinical information very challenging. As for therapy, there is no established effective treatment at this point. While some patients respond to steroid therapy, in general, collagen deposits tend to thicken with continuing formation over time, and the condition usually does not improve in most patients.

Most cases of eosinophilic gastritis, as discussed at the beginning of the lecture, represent a part of eosinophilic gastroenteritis, which is a systemic hypersensitivity disorder that can affect any part of the GI tract, including the pancreaticobiliary system, even though gastric involvement is the most common. An important clue to the diagnosis is that the patient responds very well to corticosteroid therapy. If a patient does not respond to corticosteroid therapy and continues to show increased eosinophilic infiltrate, then alternative etiologies for increased eosinophils in the stomach must be considered.

segments.transcript: I'm going to talk about different types of gastritis, which can be categorized into four broad categories based on the extent and type of inflammation within the lamina propria, as well as other unique features. The first group of gastritis is characterized by primary inflammation within the lamina propria, and depending on the type of inflammation, you have a very different differential diagnosis. For instance, if the biopsy shows very prominent lymphoplasmacytic or lymphocytic infiltrate, then your main differential diagnosis includes H. pylori gastritis and autoimmune gastritis. If the inflammation is predominantly eosinophilic, then you have to think about eosinophilic gastritis. However, if the biopsy shows prominent neutrophilic inflammation with abundant bacterial organisms, then you have to think about bacterial infection in the form of acute suppurative gastritis or emphysematous gastritis; also, toxic/chemical-induced gastritis often presents with prominent neutrophilic inflammation. The second group of gastritis is characterized by granulomatous inflammation. Obviously, the classic examples in this category include Crohn's disease and sarcoidosis. But other infectious diseases, such as tuberculosis or cryptococcus, Anisakiasis, or tapeworm, may present with granulomatous inflammation. A third category of gastritis is characterized by very limited inflammation within the lamina propria. The classic example in this category includes reactive gastropathy, which represents a nonspecific response to a lot of different mucosal irritants, including bile reflux, NSAIDs, and alcohol. Reactive gastropathy has very characteristic histologic features with foveolar hyperplasia and a corkscrew appearance, so I'm going to show you what that looks like later on. Also, some rare entities such as GVHD, chemo-radiation-induced gastritis, or drug-induced injury secondary to Colchicine and Taxol may present with very limited inflammation within the lamina propria. The final category of gastritis is defined by the presence of pigment or crystal deposition. The classic example in this category includes iron pill-induced gastritis, but some rare entities such as gastric amyloidosis, calcinosis, lanthanum carbonate, or calcium polystyrene sulfonate may potentially mimic iron pigment or deposition. So we're going to talk about all of these in this presentation.

segments.transcript: For pathologists, it's helpful to consider the causes of secondary hepatic fat, categorizing them as either macrovesicular or microvesicular fat. Macrovesicular fat, the typical type, consists of large or small fat droplets that may displace the nucleus. Secondary causes of macrovesicular fat include excess alcohol (alcohol-associated liver disease), hepatitis C, Wilson disease, malnutrition, starvation, TPN, and certain medications. Microvesicular fat, which looks different with a foamy change in hepatocytes and can be subtle, is seen in Reye syndrome, acute fatty liver of pregnancy, and with specific medications. The general category of steatotic liver disease primarily addresses macrovesicular fat, with microvesicular fat being a distinct, often more diffuse, presentation. The distinct importance of calling out NASH or MASH is because biopsy is the only definitive way to predict progression and the risk of progression to cirrhosis, liver failure, and rarely, hepatocellular carcinoma. Patients with NAFL, meaning a liver biopsy showing fat but no significant inflammation of hepatocytes, have a minimal risk of progression to cirrhosis. This applies to most individuals with fat in their liver. Some data suggests an increased risk for patients who have two of three features, such as inflammation, but their risk or progression rate is still much lower.

segments.transcript: Hirschsprung disease is relatively common, and you will encounter cases during residency. Its incidence is approximately 1 in 5,000 newborns. Hirschsprung disease is defined by the congenital absence of ganglion cells in the myenteric and submucosal plexuses of the terminal rectum, extending for a variable length into contiguous proximal bowel. This means the absence of ganglion cells may be limited to just the distal 2-3 centimeters of the rectum, which is referred to as very short segment Hirschsprung disease. If it extends further proximally but is limited to the rectosigmoid, it is referred to as short segment Hirschsprung disease. The majority of patients (about 80%) fall under short segment HD. Colonic Hirschsprung disease refers to involvement up through the descending colon, not necessarily the entire colon. Long segment refers to involvement proximal to the splenic flexure of the colon. The disease always starts distally, and its classification depends on how far it extends proximally. There have been several cases of total colonic aganglionosis or Hirschsprung disease, where the entire colon lacks ganglion cells in both plexuses. Some of these patients may also have small bowel involvement; a recent case showed involvement through the jejunum. Skip areas can be present, though not commonly seen.

segments.transcript: The neurons and glia of the enteric nervous system are derived from neural crest cells. These cells populate the gut during embryogenesis by proceeding rostrocaudally, meaning they start proximally and extend towards the distal portions of the GI tract as the fetus develops. Hirschsprung disease, often seen in the distal-most portion, is a failure of these neural crest cells to fully colonize the gut during embryogenesis. Hirschsprung disease is multi-genic and has incomplete penetrance. The multigenic nature and incomplete penetrance of Hirschsprung disease (HD) unfortunately prohibit providing a prenatal diagnosis. The majority of patients (about 70%) present with isolated aganglionosis, meaning it is the only finding, and most of these patients have a mutation in the RET gene. For example, a patient yesterday was found to have a RET gene mutation. Regarding other associated abnormalities, 12% have karyotypic abnormalities, which will be discussed further. Another 18% of patients may be genetically normal but have additional anomalies, often part of a long list of associated genetic syndromes. Most of these genetic syndromes are rare, but Down syndrome (Trisomy 21) is a frequently encountered condition. The reported incidence of Hirschsprung disease in Down syndrome is 2 to 15%, which is a relatively high number.

segments.transcript: The diagnosis of Hirschsprung disease typically involves evaluating either submucosal or myenteric ganglia. Submucosal ganglia are sampled via a suction rectal biopsy, which is commonly performed endoscopically. Seromuscular biopsy, used to look at myenteric ganglia, requires entering the abdomen and is less common for initial diagnosis. There are three minimal criteria for diagnosis: first, the absence of ganglion cells, which requires an adequate biopsy. Second, this diagnosis can only be made after extensive sectioning of the specimen. Third, the presence of hypertrophic nerve fibers may be an associated finding, though this is primarily assessed in submucosal nerves in young infants.

segments.transcript: Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis (HAEC) is a major complication and the most important cause of mortality in Hirschsprung disease. There is an increased risk for HAEC with a delay in diagnosis, an increased length of the aganglionic segment, and in patients with Trisomy 21. The incidence is variable, but mortality can be up to 30%. It is important to clearly document its presence or absence. HAEC can occur before surgical resection, within 20 months after a pull-through procedure, and unfortunately, in both aganglionic and ganglionated bowel. Therefore, it is crucial to examine the mucosa of all sections, even though focus is often placed on the submucosa and muscularis propria in Hirschsprung cases. The clinical presentation includes abdominal distension, vomiting, fever, lethargy, and shock, indicating a severe condition that clinicians should be aware of. The pathology of HAEC can range from mild acute colitis to full-blown mucosal ischemic necrosis. It can present with a pseudomembranous appearance, and in neonates, may suggest necrotizing enterocolitis with associated pneumatosis intestinalis. Treatment typically involves rectal irrigation, antibiotics, and additional biopsies to ensure there is no residual aganglionosis. In a nutshell. And then, this second part, as I mentioned, I will talk about a little.

segments.transcript: Age is important when considering the differential for malignant liver tumors in children. The tumors most common in infancy (up to one year of age) include Hepatoblastoma and malignant rhabdoid tumor. In early childhood (up to about three years of age), Hepatoblastoma remains the most common, with rhabdomyosarcoma occurring rarely as a primary liver tumor in this age range. In late childhood (up to about ten years of age, past three), Hepatocellular carcinoma becomes more common. Undifferentiated embryonal sarcoma of the liver (UESL) tends to occur in late childhood. Sarcoma and cholangiocarcinoma can occur in children but are exceedingly rare. In adolescence, Hepatocellular carcinoma is dominant, with a significant number of fibrolamellar carcinoma cases also observed. This is an extensive list of conditions associated with Hepatoblastoma; however, the key takeaway is that it's not necessary to remember all of them.

segments.transcript: Lymphocytic colitis shares many overlapping features with collagenous colitis and presents with a triad of features: an increase in intraepithelial lymphocytes, usually greater than 20 lymphocytes per 100 epithelial cells, surface epithelial injury, and increased lamina propria cellularity. While there is significant overlap with collagenous colitis, the presence of significant thickening of sub-epithelial collagen typically points to a diagnosis of collagenous colitis. Like collagenous colitis, lymphocytic colitis can have IBD-like features such as cryptitis in approximately 30% of patients, which tends to be more focal and mild. This distinction is crucial, as IBD-like features should not be predominant, and ulceration is rare. If a patient presents with bloody diarrhea rather than watery diarrhea, IBD should be considered over lymphocytic colitis. However, distinguishing between the two can be complex due to shared histological features, such as intraepithelial lymphocytes in Crohn's disease, and some evidence suggests potential transitions between microscopic colitis and IBD, though this is infrequently observed.

segments.transcript: Collagenous colitis presents with a spectrum of histological findings, though no single feature is pathognomonic. Characteristically, there is a thickened, irregular sub-epithelial collagen layer, usually greater than 10 microns and potentially up to 60 microns, showing entrapment of capillaries and inflammatory cells. Other features include intraepithelial lymphocytosis and surface epithelial damage, often manifesting as nuclear changes, degeneration, or sloughing and stripping of the epithelial layer. While a normal architectural pattern may be observed, collagenous colitis can also exhibit features overlapping with inflammatory bowel disease, such as neutrophilic inflammation, Paneth cell metaplasia, and rarely, ulceration. The presence of any of these features does not exclude a diagnosis of microscopic colitis. This image shows a case of collagenous colitis. There are a few lymphocytes in the overlying epithelium, and thickening of the sub-epithelial collagen layer with some entrapped vessels. Underneath that, there are increased inflammatory cells in the lamina propria, including plasma cells and some scattered neutrophils.

segments.transcript: There are three histologic subtypes of IPMN, with the gastric subtype being the most common. In the gastric subtype, cells become very columnar with a pale pink cytoplasmic mucin that resembles the lining of the stomach. The intestinal subtype resembles a colonic adenoma, featuring columnar cells, a slightly bluer mucin, and pseudostratification of the nuclei, similar to what is seen in a tubular adenoma (TA). The least common of the three subtypes is pancreatobiliary, which is typically a diffusely high-grade region characterized by a much higher nuclear-to-cytoplasmic (NC) ratio and more atypical features and mitotic activity.

segments.transcript: There are two different categories of primary pancreatic neoplasms: solid and cystic. In the solid category, the vast majority of tumors seen are ductal adenocarcinoma, characterized by individual glands within a desmoplastic stroma, though these will not be discussed today. Other solid tumor types, mainly composed of cellular sheets with minimal stroma, include neuroendocrine tumors (which are frequently encountered), less common solid pseudopapillary neoplasms, and much less common acinar cell carcinoma and pancreatoblastoma. In the cystic category, there are three main tumor types, in addition to pseudocysts which are typically associated with chronic pancreatitis but usually not seen in pathology. The three main cystic tumor types are intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMN), mucinous cystic neoplasm (MCN), and serous cystadenoma. These cystic and the lesser common solid types are what will be the focus. The approach is similar to IPMN: a non-invasive MCN is typically cured with surgery, but the presence of an invasive component leads to a poor prognosis. segments.transcript: Pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia is a dysplasia or a pre-invasive lesion of the pancreatic duct. There is a progression from normal to low grade, which includes PanIN-1 and PanIN-2, then to high grade, and eventually to invasive carcinoma. This progression has been molecularly defined. KRAS mutations are seen in almost all PanIN-1 lesions. As it progresses, it typically gains CDKN2A mutations or deletions and TP53 mutations, especially as it progresses to invasive carcinoma. In clinical reports, Pancreatic Intraepithelial Neoplasia (PanIN) is divided into low-grade, which, at its lowest grade, can resemble the gastric subtype of Intraductal Papillary Mucinous Neoplasm (IPMN). Low-grade PanIN exhibits some epithelial changes but typically retains basally located nuclei. High-grade PanIN, however, shows a significant loss of nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios, meaning the nucleus occupies most of the cell with very little cytoplasm. The original definition differentiates IPMN and PanIN.

segments.transcript: Fundic gland polyps are characterized by the presence of single or multiple dilated fundic glands, as seen here, lined by an attenuated layer of chief cells, parietal cells, or foveolar epithelium. Sporadic fundic gland polyps and drug-associated fundic gland polyps are considered non-neoplastic because they rarely demonstrate APC mutations, and only about 5% of these lesions have associated dysplasia. By contrast, FAP-associated fundic gland polyps are considered neoplastic because they frequently demonstrate APC mutations, and up to 50% of cases may be associated with dysplasia, even though they rarely give rise to invasive adenocarcinoma. An example of a fundic gland polyp without any evidence of dysplasia shows several dilated fundic glands lined by an attenuated layer of chief or parietal cells. Another case shows a fundic gland polyp with dilated fundic glands lined by attenuated chief cells, but with a focus of dysplastic transformation, characterized by enlarged cells with rounder nuclei and a loss of polarity.

segments.transcript: Gastric epithelial dysplasia, or adenoma, is a very rare condition, accounting for less than one percent of all gastric polyps. The term 'adenoma' technically describes a polypoid lesion, whereas 'dysplasia' means a flat lesion, but these terms are commonly used interchangeably in the literature. Most gastric adenomas present as single, sessile lesions less than two centimeters in diameter. It is important to recognize gastric adenomas because they are thought to have high malignant potential. For instance, approximately 33 percent of low-grade gastric adenomas can be associated with advanced neoplasia, high-grade neoplasia, or cancer on follow-up. The risk of malignancy is even higher for high-grade lesions, with up to 85 percent of gastric adenomas with high-grade dysplasia potentially leading to cancer on follow-up. Therefore, it is important to recognize gastric adenomas and recommend complete excision whenever possible. Additionally, dysplasia typically requires additional surveillance biopsies to look for further lesions throughout the stomach. Gastric adenomas are categorized as either low-grade or high-grade dysplasia based on cytologic and architectural features. Low-grade dysplasia typically demonstrates cytologic features involving both crypt and surface epithelium. This example of an intestinal type gastric adenoma looks very similar to a colorectal tubular adenoma, with scattered goblet cells consistent with intestinal metaplasia. This one shows low-grade cytologic adenoma with elongated, hyperchromatic, and crowded nuclei involving both crypt and surface epithelium. By definition, low-grade dysplasia should demonstrate surface involvement by dysplastic changes. If dysplasia is limited to the crypt base without obvious surface involvement, reactive changes are favored. In support of this, an earlier study was published in HSP back in 2021.

segments.transcript: Peutz-Jeghers polyp has a very distinct morphological feature, characterized by irregular and branching bundles of smooth muscle emerging from the muscularis mucosae, covered by abundant but disorganized foveolar-like epithelium with abundant cytoplasm and cystic changes. An important thing about gastric Peutz-Jeghers polyp is that, unlike its small bowel counterpart, gastric Peutz-Jeghers polyp tends to show much thinner and less branching bundles of smooth muscle emerging from the muscularis mucosae, so it can be potentially mistaken for a hyperplastic polyp endoscopically. However, unlike the hyperplastic polyp, which is characterized by increased inflammation in the lamina propria with a lot of neutrophil infiltration and ulceration, Peutz-Jeghers polyp typically shows periglandular inflammation. For example, this is another illustration of a Peutz-Jeghers polyp stained with smooth muscle actin; the smooth muscle actin highlighting the muscularis mucosae also demonstrates relatively thin and less branching bundles of smooth muscle emerging from the muscularis mucosae, unlike its small bowel counterpart. Gastric Peutz-Jeghers polyps are thought to have a very low malignant potential; in fact, only about 3% of Peutz-Jeghers polyps may show evidence of dysplasia. However, patients with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome have an increased chance of developing gastric cancer in their lifetime, up to 30%. Therefore, upper GI surveillance starts as early as 8 years of age. It's important to target polyps greater than 1 cm in diameter and completely resected lesions with regular follow-up due to their high recurrence rate.

segments.transcript: Classifying adult renal tumor types is complex, often beginning with grouping by morphological features such as clear cells or papillary morphology. Clear cell RCC is associated with 3p minus or VHL mutations. Many tumors contain clear cells, so this category can be further refined by considering factors like grade, where clear cell tumors can present as low or high grade. Papillary RCC is typically defined by c-MET amplification and common trisomies of chromosomes 7 and 17. Familial papillary RCC syndromes and Hereditary Leiomyomatosis-associated RCC (HLRCC), which also presents with papillary morphology, are important considerations. While grouping by oncocytic cytoplasm is less useful as almost any renal tumor can exhibit this feature, grade can be a distinguishing factor. Chromophobe RCC, a low-grade malignancy, can be challenging to differentiate from oncocytomas, though experienced pathologists find it more straightforward than often perceived. Collecting Duct RCC, or Bellini Duct Carcinoma, is often considered a 'waste basket' diagnosis, as molecular studies frequently reclassify these tumors into categories like HLRCC (due to fumarate hydratase mutations) or urothelial carcinomas. Renal Medullary RCC, a highly aggressive tumor associated with hemoglobinopathies, is distinguished by its central medullary location, uniformly high grade, and infiltrative growth pattern, leading to very poor prognosis. A low-grade variant, Tubular Cystic Renal Cell Carcinoma, typically occurs in males and has a better prognosis but requires monitoring. Translocation RCCs exhibit morphology intermediate between clear cell and papillary types. RCC Unclassified is reserved for cases where extensive workup fails to categorize the tumor, and should ideally be specified as high or low grade. Angiomyolipoma, a stromal tumor, can mimic various epithelial renal tumors (oncocytic, clear cell) and is recommended to be referred to as a PEComa to align with nomenclature for similar tumors elsewhere in the body.

segments.transcript: Gleason grading is one of the most important issues with prostate adenocarcinoma after diagnosis. It is the most important tissue-based prognostic and predictive biomarker in prostate cancer, with grade often being a bigger driver than stage in this context. Although developed in the 1960s, the Gleason system was not accepted by the World Health Organization until 2003, taking 30 years to gain global consensus. It predicts stage, treatment outcomes, recurrence, progression, and death better than other available methods, making its correct application crucial. Gleason grading has profound effects on management, especially regarding the presence of pattern four or greater, which typically indicates true cancer requiring treatment. If only pattern three is present, active surveillance may be considered. The grade influences types of radiation, the use of anti-androgen or other chemotherapy with radiation, and the decision for adjuvant therapy post-prostatectomy, which often involves a combination of radiation to the prostate bed and regional lymph nodes with anti-androgens for high-grade cases.

segments.transcript: I want to share my philosophy about grading malignancies in general before continuing the lecture, as it's really important. Grading of malignancies originated with squamous cell carcinomas in the head and neck region in the 1920s. It was proposed that the degree of differentiation observed under the microscope correlates with patient outcomes, making grading a strong prognostic and predictive biomarker. Most grading systems are usually a three-tiered system, categorizing tumors into baskets based on their degree of differentiation. For example, a tumor where it's difficult to distinguish between a benign condition (like liver adenoma or pseudo hyperplasia) and a well-differentiated carcinoma (hepatocellular or squamous) would typically be a Grade 1. A tumor that is so poorly differentiated that its origin or type is uncertain, but ultimately identified as a primary, would be a Grade 3. Everything in between these extremes is a Grade 2. This first approximation helps avoid the subjectivity often associated with grading. One of the main problems with grading is its inherent subjectivity. This is an area where artificial intelligence and image analysis could significantly impact pathology practice, as these morphologic nuances are difficult for humans to consistently interpret. Pathologists can develop grading systems by either quantifying various tumor criteria (like nuclear size, mitoses, cell size, or glandular formation) across many tumors and correlating them with outcomes, or by creating a series of cartoons depicting different tumor growth patterns, then matching real tumors to these cartoons and correlating with outcomes—a method similar to the Gleason system. AI can analyze many more features objectively to create more granular grading systems. Thus, grading is terribly subjective, leading to significant inter- and intra-observer variability, with different people applying criteria differently. There are numerous grading systems; for prostate cancer alone, over 40 published systems exist, with Gleason being widely accepted after 30 years. Sampling issues or errors are also a problem, as the sampled area might not represent the part of the tumor driving its biological behavior, which current systems cannot fully overcome. Biologically, the least differentiated area is assumed to drive tumor behavior, and most grading systems focus on identifying this worst or most poorly differentiated region, irrespective of its size, to assign the grade. Errors can occur if a high-grade area is detected but is not truly proliferative (a false positive), or if a high-grade area is an indicator that the entire tumor is aggressive, even if other areas are well-differentiated (a true positive).

segments.transcript: Now, I'm going to talk about the Gleason system because it is unique compared to how virtually all other grading systems work. It was formulated in the 1960s, validated in the 1970s, and continues to be refined today because, despite its shortcomings, it remains the most powerful prognostic and predictive indicator. Here are two things that make Gleason grading different from all other grading types: First, it's based on architecture alone; the cytology of the tumor cells doesn't matter, as it is the tumor's growth pattern that determines the grade. Second, it's one of the rare systems that accounts for tumor heterogeneity, recognizing that there are different areas with different growth patterns. Grades are synonymous with patterns, and there are five different patterns of gland growth or architecture that the Gleason system examines. To account for heterogeneity, a score (sum) is assigned based on the most common pattern (X) and the second most common pattern (Y). So, X + Y gives you the score, which ranges from 2 to 10. Score and sum are synonymous terms, as are grade and pattern; however, grade and score are not synonymous. Originally, if the secondary pattern (Y) was less than 5% (or sometimes between 3-5%) of the total tumor, the primary pattern (X) was repeated (X+X). In the modern era, however, if the secondary pattern (Y) is grade four or five, it is included in the score even if it constitutes less than 5% because it correlates with outcomes and disease behavior. This grading is applied only to primary tumors, not treated or metastatic ones, as the system is designed to predict for metastases. The architectural assessment is done at low power, verified at high power if needed. Understanding Gleason grading is critical for subsequent discussions.

segments.transcript: This discussion covers the history of different prostate specimens and factors that have changed urologic and pathologic practice. Four groundbreaking changes in the late 1980s and early 1990s revolutionized prostate care. First, the development of serum PSA by Dr. Stamey at Stanford allowed for earlier detection of prostate cancer, contrasting with previous methods that relied on symptoms like urinary obstruction requiring TURP, or discovery through metastatic disease like fractures or anemia, followed by biopsy of metastatic deposits. Elevated serum PSA became an indicator for prostate cancer. Second, the development of TRUS (transrectal ultrasound) biopsies, utilizing transducers from Japan, enabled targeted needle core biopsies. Dr. Stamey, along with urologist John McNeil, developed the initial algorithms for treating prostate cancer based on correlations between serum PSA and TRUS biopsy findings; McNeil is considered the father of prostate pathology despite being a urologist. Third, Patrick Walsh at Johns Hopkins developed a nerve-sparing radical prostatectomy technique that significantly reduced morbidity, including preventing impotence and improving continence rates, making curative surgery more viable. Fourth, the introduction of 5-alpha reductase inhibitors (finasteride and dutasteride) for treating Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH) drastically reduced the number of TURP specimens pathologists processed daily, as BPH could now be medically managed. Before TRUS biopsies, FNAs (fine needle aspirates) of the prostate were used, but these lacked the ability to apply the Gleason system for tumor grading, often leading directly to radical prostatectomy. Current specimens include needle biopsies, prostatectomy specimens, and increasingly, biopsies of metastatic sites. While historically, elevated serum PSA after prostatectomy and scans showing bone lesions definitively indicated metastatic prostate cancer without requiring biopsy, the paradigm is shifting. Future practices may involve biopsying metastases to guide new treatments, though liquid biopsies for detecting markers in blood could also obviate the need for tissue biopsies. These advancements are expected to drastically change prostate pathology in the next 5-10 years.

For instance, atrophic adenocarcinomas can resemble benign atrophy, pseudohyperplastic tumors may look like benign hyperplasia, and foamy gland type cancer can be mistaken for benign Cowper's glands. segments.transcript: I always start off with the list of tumors for these lectures. It is important to have the list of all the different possibilities or the most common possibilities for all the tumors. I try to break these things down into clusters that hopefully make it easier to think about. For prostate tumors, we are primarily talking about prostatic (small acinar) adenocarcinoma, which accounts for virtually every tumor that occurs in the prostate gland. This is a tumor of the secretory cells of the prostate acini. While this will be the main focus, other tumor types exist. Most of these other types are covered in other areas and are pointed out for completeness. Prostatic (small acinar) adenocarcinoma is unique to the prostate gland and does not occur anywhere else in the body. In contrast, most other tumor types can occur in other places. When these other tumor types occur in the prostate gland, they are virtually all considered high-grade tumors, with the rare exception of basal cell carcinomas or adenoid cystic carcinoma of the prostate gland. These incredibly rare tumors of the basal cell layer are usually considered low-grade. Small cell carcinoma is becoming more commonly seen in the prostate gland or in the genitourinary world. When present, even as a small component of another tumor, it needs to be diagnosed because it requires different treatment. It appears that new drugs, likely oncology-wide, are pushing tumors towards a small cell phenotype, making it more probable for treated, metastatic prostatic adenocarcinomas to recur as small cell. Sarcomatoid carcinomas, typically associated with urothelial carcinoma, can also occur in the prostate gland. It probably does not matter if they originate from urothelial or adenocarcinoma, as they are aggressive and need to be treated as high-grade tumors. Tumors that occur in the urinary bladder or urethra, such as urothelial carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, or intestinal type adenocarcinoma, can infiltrate the prostate gland or prostatic urethra. Finally, there is a list of stromal tumors, which are rare, including sarcomas, lymphomas, and melanoma. Additionally, there is STUMP (Stromal Tumor of Uncertain Malignant Potential), unique to the prostate gland, which is a proliferation of stromal cells with features intermediate between benign stromal hyperplasia and sarcoma. The entire lecture will primarily focus on prostatic adenocarcinoma.

segments.transcript: The choice between radiation therapy and prostatectomy is a critical decision. Generally, younger patients are treated with prostatectomy, while older patients receive radiation. This approach is favored because irradiating a younger patient can lead to long-term side effects. Furthermore, if a prostatectomy fails, radiation remains a viable backup treatment. Conversely, if radiation is used as the primary treatment and fails, subsequent radiation as a backup plan is significantly delayed, potentially by 10 years. This section primarily addresses the treatment of prostate cancer recurrence, where therapies used for primary treatment also come into play as salvage treatments. These may include a salvage prostatectomy or salvage radiation, especially if an initial prostatectomy failed. If patients are not candidates for these, hormone therapies are administered, which carries the risk of developing castrate resistance. Other available therapies are also considered.

Often, benign tissue in treated prostate biopsies presents visual cues, allowing pathologists to identify treated cases even without prior knowledge. Treated prostate cancer, whether by radiation or anti-androgen therapy, can cause atrophic or metaplastic changes in both benign and tumor tissue. These changes include reactionary basal cell hyperplasia, squamous metaplasia, or clear cell development in benign areas, serving as indicators of prior treatment. Prostate cancer and secretory cells in treated settings might weakly display basal cell markers, unlike the strong staining seen in neighboring basal cells. Crucially, most prostate cancer markers like PSA, PSAP, and PSMA typically become weaker post-treatment. However, NKX3.1 usually strengthens, and while androgen receptor also strengthens, it is not specific due to positivity in basal cells.

segments.transcript: For grading prostate cancers, there are more than 40 grading systems in the literature; however, Gleason has proven itself to be the most effective and useful. One of our colleagues, Dr. Jesse McKenny at Cleveland Clinic Foundation, is actually working on a new grading system, though it might get superseded by robots before he finishes. Grading systems are designed in two ways: one is by drawing patterns observed and then looking at the outcomes for each to determine the most and least aggressive patterns, and the other is by selecting a bunch of histologic criteria to examine, such as counting mitotic figures, nuclear size, or degree of differentiation. Most grading systems are composed of a combination of growth or architecture and cytology. The Gleason system, however, has two unique aspects: it is based solely on architecture, which is rare for most grading systems, meaning it requires tissue sections and cannot be used with cytology specimens; and it takes into account tumor heterogeneity, while most other systems focus only on the area that is least differentiated or has the highest grade score.

Due to political reasons, even though Gleason's scheme was developed in the late 1960s, it was not accepted by the World Health Organization until 2003. It is surprising that its adoption took so long. The Gleason score predicts stage, treatment outcomes, chances of recurrence, progression, and death better than anything else. It has profound effects on management, influencing decisions such as active surveillance, where high-grade patterns are undesirable. For radiation therapy, higher-grade patterns necessitate the addition of anti-androgens, which is not required for lower-grade patterns. I will explain high-grade and low-grade patterns shortly. Furthermore, the decision to administer adjuvant therapy after a prostatectomy is entirely driven by the Gleason score.

segments.transcript: The original Gleason system, developed in the 1960s and validated in the 1970s, continues to be modified and refined today. It focuses solely on architectural growth patterns, not cytologic features, to account for tumor heterogeneity. The original system utilized five grades or patterns. A score is derived by summing the most common pattern or grade (the primary grade, X) and the second most common pattern or grade (the secondary grade, Y). Score and sum are synonymous terms, as are grade and pattern, though it is important to distinguish between grade and score. If the secondary pattern constitutes less than 5% or 3% (depending on the specific study), the primary grade (X) is repeated, resulting in a score of two X's. This system is designed for primary tumors only, not for treated tumors or metastases, as it is prognostic for recurrence and the development of metastatic disease.

segments.transcript: I have just gone through all those different subtypes and stressed that it is the growth pattern that matters, not the subtype or variant. The Gleason system has been modified since its original description. The International Society of Urologic Pathologists (ISUP) held two consensus meetings in 2005 and 2014 to discuss these modifications, bringing together prostate pathologists to identify common areas, make consensus statements, and clarify areas of confusion through experiments. The 2005 recommendations were initially criticized for lacking outcome data. Specifically, cribriform growth patterns, previously considered pattern three, were reclassified into pattern four. Subsequent outcome studies conducted between 2005 and 2014 validated most of these changes in practice and significantly increased consistency among pathologists regarding cribriform grading. This addressed the problems with the original system. Some patterns are extremely rare, and it's questionable if grade one and grade two truly represent cancer. When the system was developed, IHC was not available. As mentioned, grade two is rare and difficult to diagnose on a needle core. Consequently, the system was modified, recommending that nothing should be classified as grade one, and grade two should almost never be assigned, instead classifying it as grade three. Some descriptions were vague, such as cribriform three versus cribriform four. There wasn't a good cutoff back then, so we just categorized them all as four, which actually helped. Additionally, not all growth patterns were represented in the original Gleason system; for example, glomerulations were categorized as four, perhaps incorrectly, due to their complex growth.

segments.transcript: According to the ISUP modifications to Gleason scoring, if a tumor consists of 95% patterns 4 and 5 with less than 5% pattern 3, the pattern 3 component is ignored, resulting in a 4+4 score. In the prostate, discrete tumors should be scored separately, especially when grades are disparate, as the highest-grade component drives the outcome. For instance, a 4+5 separate tumor alongside a large 3+3 lesion should be graded as 4+5 to accurately reflect prognosis. Additionally, based on UCSF's work, reporting the percentage of patterns greater than pattern 3 was recommended. However, at UCSF, this recommendation is not followed; tertiary patterns are still reported. This practice is maintained specifically for research purposes, as dropping the tertiary pattern would result in a loss of valuable information necessary for robust studies and differentiating tumors.

This is confusing for patients and difficult to explain, leading to significant anxiety; for example, telling a patient they have a 'six' and a 'great outcome' can be met with confusion and fear, as patients perceive six as being 'past halfway' on the scoring system, leading to distress. Another issue is that under the modified Gleason system, a score of 3+4 and 4+3 are numerically the same (7), but their clinical outcomes are very different. This is critical because grade four indicates a higher likelihood of true cancer compared to grade three; thus, a predominant grade four component (4+3) suggests a worse prognosis. A 4+3 Gleason score is Grade Group three. Any Gleason score of eight is Grade Group four, and anything above eight is Grade Group five. UCSF does not include this translation in their reports because it is a simple conversion from a Gleason score to a Grade Group, widely understood by practitioners. This system has been extensively validated and is endorsed by the World Health Organization and the College of American Pathologists. Regarding UCSF's specific application of this data, they note that 4+3 and 4+4 are considered the same, implying that Gleason scores of eight fall into Grade Group three. Additionally, their Grade Group five specifically refers to 5+5 scores, while Grade Group four encompasses any score of nine. To apply Grade Groups, the Gleason system was originally developed using the highest scored biopsy. For instance, if multiple biopsies included a four plus five, that would be used. Subsequent studies have shown that using the overall grade for all biopsies in a case actually works better, though both methods are acceptable. In prostatectomy, with a Grade 5 component greater than five percent, this should be made the secondary pattern in the prostatectomy score. Some institutions, however, report tertiary patterns. Grade Groups represent a simple translation from the Gleason score, and some institutions choose not to include them in reports to maintain clarity and reduce confusion.

segments.transcript: Angiomyolipomas (AMLs) are often referred to as PEComas, as they can occur in various body sites, not just the kidney. These are typically triphasic tumors with angio, myo, and lipo components, though they can sometimes present with only one phase, such as an epithelioid or myoid appearance. The vessels in these tumors lack elastica, which can be a distinguishing feature when considering vascular tumors. While usually benign, they can sometimes exhibit bizarre nuclei or pleomorphism, prompting consideration of a malignant angiomyolipoma. Immunohistochemistry is characteristic: they are positive for melanocytic markers (like HMB-45) but negative for S100 and keratin. Epithelioid variants often stain positive for smooth muscle actin. Approximately half of kidney-involved cases are associated with Tuberous Sclerosis, with mutations in either the TSC-1 or TSC-2 genes, a common topic for board questions.

segments.transcript: When evaluating a testicular tumor, understanding its relation to surrounding tissues is crucial for staging. If a tumor is next to fat, it likely indicates involvement of higher sub-tissue, classifying it as pT2. Gross evaluation plays a very important role in staging, as microscopic differentiation between the epididymis and rete testis can be challenging. Microscopically, the epididymis has a round contour of tubular structures lined by columnar cells with ample cytoplasm. In contrast, the rete testis is lined by very flat epithelial cells and has a reticulated architecture. If a tumor invades the rete testis within the tubular space without entering the stroma, it is classified as pT1. Practical tips include maintaining a clean workspace and knife to prevent carryover, always taking margins first before cutting into the tumor, and generously submitting hilar sections to ensure proper staging. The final staging of testicular tumors also heavily depends on the number and size of involved lymph node metastases.

segments.transcript: We will review normal testicular histology. Two panels depict non-neoplastic normal adult testes, where seminiferous tubules are mostly back-to-back with minimal intervening stroma; occasional edema may be present, but not scarring. In a normal adult testis, Leydig cells are typically inconspicuous, appearing as pink, island-like clusters between the seminiferous tubules. However, in an atrophic testis, as shown in the right panel, Leydig cells can become more prominent, even when the atrophy is non-neoplastic. Severely atrophic tubules can make Leydig cells appear so prominent that they might be mistaken for a Leydig cell tumor. It is crucial to check the patient's history and the background testicular tissue, as prominent Leydig cells are not necessarily neoplastic. Prepubertal testes, in contrast, look very different. They still exhibit mostly back-to-back seminiferous tubules, but within the tubules, one will primarily observe immature Sertoli cells and sometimes germ cells, though germ cells are challenging to identify with routine microscopy. Special stains can confirm germ cell presence, but their mere existence does not indicate neoplasia. Therefore, correlating findings with patient age is vital for an accurate diagnosis. The presentation will then move on to abnormal testes, with a further illustration of adult normal testes.

Instead, it is probably wise to select one representative block that displays the most patterns you observe, and then perform about three targeted immunohistochemical (IHC) stains on it to aid your diagnosis. Additionally, it is beneficial to practice interpreting these findings independently, without immediate supervision, especially for identifying specific types like seminoma. Seminoma cells tend to have very clear and pale cytoplasm with a large nucleus and prominent nucleoli. The cells are often polygonal, with clear borders, sometimes appearing box-like. They tend to be discohesive, but sometimes they can be quite cohesive, so cohesion is not your only clue. When diagnosing Seminoma, immunohistochemistry (IHC) is useful. You can use OCT3/4 and SOX2; OCT3/4 should be positive, and SOX2 should be negative.

segments.transcript: When addressing tumors of the urinary bladder, ureter, or renal pelvis, patients often present with blood in their urine, which prompts immediate medical attention. While benign conditions can cause this, malignancy is a significant concern. A urologist will typically use a cystoscope to examine the urethra and bladder for lesions, which could appear as flat red patches, papillary tumors, or polypoid masses. After identifying and removing the mass, the pathologist determines the tumor type and extent of invasion, which informs the patient's treatment plan. Specimen types for the urinary system include urine cytology, where malignant cells confirm a cancer diagnosis. Sometimes, bladder washings are performed to dislodge atypical cells for easier cytological diagnosis. Small biopsies are taken, especially from red patches, to rule out irritation. Transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT) involves surgically removing visible bladder tumors. Other resections include simple or segmental resections of the ureter, urethra, bladder, or urachus. In cases requiring a radical resection, the entire urinary bladder is removed along with the distal ends of the ureters, and either the prostate in male patients or portions of the anterior vagina in female patients.

segments.transcript: Normal urothelium is a cohesive, stratified epithelium typically five to seven cell layers thick. While it can be thicker (suggesting hyperplasia) or thinner (due to denudation by instrumentation, which is important to note as carcinoma can also cause denudation), its normal appearance is key. The layer in contact with the basement membrane is a small basal cell layer containing stem cells, which can have a high nucleocytoplasmic ratio and are small, often resembling lymphocytes. While not always visible, their presence helps orient the viewer to the layers above. After the basal layer, cells exhibit maturing growth, becoming progressively more mature as they reach the surface, typically increasing their cytoplasm and maintaining a nucleus one to three times the size of a lymphocyte. Mitoses in normal urothelium should be confined to the basal layer or just above it; their presence closer to the surface may indicate malignancy. Finally, umbrella cells are found on the surface; these can appear atypical, degenerating, or hyperchromatic, but if observed only on the surface, they are typically benign.

segments.transcript: Regarding flat lesions in the urinary bladder, completely normal tissue is distinct from hyperplasia, which we classify as urothelial proliferation of uncertain malignant potential (UPUMP). Other categories include reactive atypia. In the WHO book, dysplasia is discussed, but at UCSF, we avoid this term due to historical grading systems, specifically ISUP in urologic pathology. Older systems graded dysplasia as high-grade and low-grade; using 'dysplasia' now often leads to confusion, as high-grade dysplasia was analogous to carcinoma in situ (CIS), while low-grade dysplasia in the old system corresponds to dysplasia in the new. To prevent misinterpretation, UCSF classifies such ambiguous cases as atypia, specifically stating that features are lacking for a definitive diagnosis of CIS but are suspicious for it. Atypia of unknown significance, even if inflamed with neutrophils, is also categorized under atypia at UCSF, necessitating follow-up. Additionally, papillary hyperplasia, which presents with a 'tending look,' fits under the UPUMP diagnostic category.

segments.transcript: Similar to flat lesions, papillary lesions have undergone various iterations of grading schemes over the years. Historically, there have been numerous grading systems, many of which incorporated grade one, grade two, and grade three categories. However, these schemes often led pathologists to classify most cases into the grade two category, rendering them largely unusable. While approaches like Dr. Bill Murphy's, which categorized lesions as Papilloma, low grade, and high grade, were favored by some, the current standard system used is the WHO/ISUP system, developed around 1990. This system includes classifications such as Papilloma (benign), low malignant potential (LMP) as an intermediate category, low grade, and high grade. Pathologists may still encounter older grading schemes in confirmed or consult cases, indicating that those pathologists are not current with the significant changes in grading systems over the last 30 years.

segments.transcript: Epithelioid leiomyoma is a diagnosis of exclusion, requiring consideration and ruling out of several other conditions. PEComa (perivascular epithelioid cell tumor) is a key differential, with a morphological spectrum that can mimic both leiomyoma and leiomyosarcoma. For the purposes of this discussion, we will focus on the bland end of the PEComa spectrum. Other entities to consider include epithelioid variants of endometrial stromal tumors, which can be identified using CD10 or genetic alterations like JAZF1 and PHF1. Carcinomas, such as clear cell or endometrioid carcinoma, can also present with oncocytic or epithelioid features. It's important to remember that uterine corpus-based lesions may originate from the cervix, such as squamous cell carcinoma, which can extend into the endometrium or endomyometrium. In premenopausal patients, trophoblastic tumors like placental site trophoblastic tumor or epithelioid trophoblastic tumor, and even some monophasic choriocarcinomas, can mimic epithelioid smooth muscle tumors. Melanoma should also be included in the differential diagnosis. PEComa is a rare mesenchymal tumor of uncertain cell origin, found in various sites including the uterus, and characterized by a dual melanocytic and myoid immunophenotype. Molecular classification reveals mutations in TSC1 or TSC2, or translocations involving TFE3 and RAD51 in about half of cases, with a minority remaining unclassifiable. Distinguishing PEComa from smooth muscle tumors is crucial because approximately a third of PEComas recur, some fatally, and the risk stratification criteria differ. Furthermore, PEComas are part of a larger tumor family that includes PLAM (pulmonary lymphangioleiomyomatosis) and renal angiomyolipomas. Identifying PEComa can alert clinicians to the potential for other PEComa-related tumors. Patients with TSC mutations are at risk for tuberous sclerosis complex, and a PEComa diagnosis may be the index finding, necessitating evaluation for TSC. Finally, PEComas with TSC mutations are amenable to targeted therapy, such as mTOR inhibitors, which is distinct from leiomyosarcoma, for which no targeted therapies are currently available. Therefore, accurate differentiation is essential for appropriate patient management and treatment.

We need to determine if we are looking at some form of hyperplasia or a low-grade form of carcinoma. Of course, this is much more complicated than these two diagnostic possibilities, as there are many more additional entities to consider. This is also complicated by interpretive problems and diagnostic pitfalls, all of which I will cover in this session. With that introduction to management, let's look at clinically relevant differential diagnosis based on the pattern of the gland crowding. Is it glandular? Is it papillary, or is it predominantly mucin-rich? When considering glandular pattern crowding, we must account for benign, pre-cancerous, and low-risk cancers, as well as high-risk cancers like serous carcinoma and mesonephric-like carcinoma that can present with a glandular pattern. It's also important to note that tumors originating outside the uterus, such as endocervical and colorectal adenocarcinomas, can secondarily involve the endometrium and mimic low-grade endometrial carcinoma.

segments.transcript: Now, we can move on to mucin-rich variants of endometrial gland crowding. The clinically relevant differential diagnosis is extensive, ranging from benign entities all the way up to high-risk and secondary forms of cancer. In the benign categories, there are two lesions to be aware of: number one, mucinous metaplasia; and number two, contamination of the endometrial biopsy by so-called endocervical microglandular hyperplasia (MGH). The definition of MGH is a benign alteration that occurs in the endocervix or, more commonly, in endocervical polyps, typically in pre-menopausal women who have been exposed to progestin therapy. Very importantly, this is rarely found in post-menopausal women, so paying attention to the patient's age becomes very important when you see features that you suspect are MGH. Even though this is a cervical-based alteration, it can show up in endometrial biopsies as a contaminant. The criteria for this diagnosis are the following: you will see crowded, cribriform endocervical glands; there will be an admixture of squamous metaplasia and/or reserve cell hyperplasia; within the lumen of these glands, you often see mucin and neutrophils; and the epithelium often has vacuolization or microcystic spaces. So, why is this a diagnostic problem? It's a problem because this morphology can resemble MGH-like features of endometrial cancers that can occur in older women. Therefore, if you have an endometrial biopsy from a post-menopausal patient that has what you think is just contamination by MGH, use caution, because that may actually be the tip of the iceberg of an MGH-like endometrial cancer.

segments.transcript: Adenoid cystic carcinoma is graded based on the percentage of its solid component, with 30% serving as a key cut-off. If there is no solid component, it is considered low grade (Grade 1, predominantly tubular). If the solid component is less than 30%, it is intermediate grade (Grade 2), and if greater than 30%, it is high grade (Grade 3). It is crucial to distinguish high-grade adenoid cystic carcinoma from adenoid cystic carcinoma with high-grade transformation. High-grade transformation carries a significantly worse prognosis because it requires additional features like solid architecture, necrosis, mitotic activity, and apoptosis, indicating a more aggressive tumor that progresses more quickly. While calling it high grade merely signifies a significant solid component, even low-grade adenoid cystic carcinomas have a poor prognosis. However, patients with low-grade tumors can often live for decades, potentially experiencing slow-growing, asymptomatic metastases, such as lung nodules, many years after initial treatment like surgery and local radiation. segments.transcript: Lichen Planus is an oral disease named by Erasmus Wilson, an 18th or 19th-century polymath, who thought the condition resembled lichen growing on rocks and trees (Plenus meaning flat). This condition affects about 1 to 2% of the adult population and is quite common, though its cause is unknown. It typically occurs in the mouth and on the skin, often together. Clinically, the oral lesions are characterized by white, lace-like patterns, usually on the buccal mucosa but also on the lips and gingiva. These intersecting lines are sometimes called reticular hyperkeratosis. When the patient is asymptomatic, no treatment is required, but when lesions become ulcerated or symptomatic, they are treated with topical steroids.

segments.transcript: There are two different kinds of cutaneous cancers that should not be included because they are staged separately: melanoma and Merkel cell carcinoma. Staging for cutaneous carcinoma is based on the greatest dimension of the primary tumor. T staging for cutaneous carcinomas categorizes tumors as carcinoma in situ, smaller than two centimeters, between two and four centimeters, or larger than four centimeters. Crucially, the presence of perineural or deep invasion significantly impacts staging. This is a critical point, as cases have been significantly understaged based on these criteria; for example, a depth of six millimeters is sufficient to reach PT3. In the skin, invasion is measured from the granular layer of the adjacent normal epidermis. Greater than six millimeters is considered deep invasion, or if it extends beyond the subcutaneous fat. Perineural invasion is also a criterion, specifically when the nerve is deeper than the dermis, or the invasion is larger than 100 micrometers, or if it presents with involvement of named nerves. Involvement of named nerves indicates large nerves, provided the invasion has not extended into the skull base, which would then be classified beyond pT4b.

In many instances, what looks like a potential subepidermal blister under the microscope is actually not discernible at all to the clinician's eye. Acantholysis is probably the most important and distinctive mechanism for blister formation, characterized by a loss of the visible cell-cell attachments of keratinocytes at the light microscopic hematoxylin and eosin level. The cells become rounded and discohesive. Acantholysis is associated with compromise of a critical component of the desmosome, which are the film strip or ladder-run type structures connecting one keratinocyte to another that are visible on H&E at the light microscopic level. Desmosomes are associated with the keratin cytoskeleton of the cell and are a much stronger structure holding cells together compared to the adherens junction and the associated actin cytoskeleton involved with spongiosis and E-cadherin. Therefore, compromise of the desmosome readily results in a loss of visible intercellular attachments and a rounding and discohesion of the keratinocytes. Most commonly, this is antibody-mediated targeting of a critical structure of the desmosome, as exemplified by all the different variants of pemphigus.

segments.transcript: Keratoacanthoma is a controversial entity in dermatology and pathology. Some authorities classify it as a distinctive variant of squamous cell carcinoma, while others consider it separate. Despite profound histologic and clinical overlap, most textbooks separate keratoacanthoma from squamous cell carcinoma. In our institution, like many others, we generally report these as squamous cell carcinoma, keratoacanthoma type. What is not controversial, however, are its distinctive clinical and histologic features. As a pathologist, evaluating a partial sampling can make it difficult or impossible to definitively diagnose keratoacanthoma. From a practical standpoint, this often necessitates clinical-pathologic correlation, which is somewhat unique among skin cancers. Clinically, keratoacanthomas typically present as rapidly growing nodules with a central keratotic core. If left untreated, these tumors usually undergo spontaneous regression, a major argument against classifying them as squamous cell carcinomas. Histologically, distinctive features include inward bending papillations (buttresses), large glassy pale eosinophilic keratinocytes, and collections of neutrophils within the epithelial component. At the advancing edge or basal layer, varying degrees of atypia are observed, from subtle to severe.

segments.transcript: Nodular basal cell carcinoma is that classic pearly-telangiectatic papule or nodule, often with a kind of a waxy appearance. In this particular image that I'm showing, notice that the center of the tumor is also ulcerated or eroded, and so I suspect there might also be an infiltrative component here. Infiltrative BCC doesn't always have as distinctive of a clinical appearance compared to superficial and nodular BCC, and often is kind of insidious. It's difficult to judge exactly how much undermining or deep extension of an infiltrative basal cell carcinoma might be present from the clinical appearances alone. Histologic hallmarks of all subtypes of basal cell carcinoma include peripheral palisading of the tumor and clefting between the tumor and adjacent stroma, typically with a myxoid and mucinous appearance. And in contrast to squamous cell carcinoma where the tumor cell cytoplasm is more or less eosinophilic or pink, the tumor cells in BCC have relatively scant cytoplasm so that the basophilia of the nucleus predominates, and the overall appearance of the tumor even from low magnification is that of more of a purple or basaloid tumor. One more comment about the subtyping of basal cell carcinoma: it is something that we as pathologists should attempt to do in every instance. It may not be possible in every case, and in that case it would be appropriate to say that the sample doesn't permit subtyping. Multiple studies have also shown that subtyping basal cells from shave and punch biopsies is not highly accurate, maybe 80 percent, so not bad, but definitely far from perfect. segments.transcript: In order to identify and appreciate histopathologic features, we need to appreciate the normal histology of skin tissue. We will start by reviewing some basic structures in the skin. As a teacher, I am particularly appreciative of those who have taught me, and this is my tribute to Dr. Marc Goldyne, a former attending dermatology physician from my training days at the Veterans Affairs Hospital in San Francisco. He is now an expert in teledermatology and is artistically talented, both musically and graphically. He made this diagram in the pre-digital age, and I am happy to use it today to teach basic skin anatomy. Starting with the epidermis, to the naked eye, it is paper-thin. As we can see in the diagram, it actually has a number of cells. It has an undulating pattern, kind of like an egg crate, interfacing with the underlying dermis. That is the whole area here, and we will focus on that in the next few slides. The epidermis contains mostly keratinocytes, but also melanocytes, Langerhans cells, Merkel cells, and occasional small trafficking lymphocytes. We will focus on the keratinocytes and the melanocytes for now. We will not discuss much about the underlying dermis or the subcutis, but we can see that the vascular and lymphatic systems, hair follicles, sebaceous glands, eccrine, and in some sites, apocrine sweat glands and ducts are present, along with an underlying subcutaneous fat layer. Keep in mind, any one of these cells can undergo controlled or uncontrolled growth, creating a benign or malignant tumor. Of course, there is also a whole world of inflammatory disorders, which we will touch on only briefly today.

Therefore, I would expect any listener to be skeptical about the ability of distinguishing actinic granuloma from GA. I am going to take a few extra minutes to delve a little bit deeper and look at some primary data, starting with this study by a dermatopathologist whom I met a long time ago in San Francisco, and whose scholarship and collegiality I have great respect for: Dr. Richard Crawford from Vancouver and colleagues. Original data from this series looks first at multinucleated giant cells, present in 100% of actinic granuloma but overall present in not quite 50% of the GA cases, both on sun-damaged and non-sun-damaged skin. segments.transcript: Dermatopathology is a relatively subspecialized area in medicine dedicated to the evaluation and management of skin disease via the microscopic and increasingly sub-microscopic evaluation of lesional skin tissue. It is a fund of knowledge created jointly through the efforts of pathologists and dermatologists about a century and a half ago. To conduct an authentic historical dive into its origins, one needs to understand some European languages. Reviewing relatively ancient textbooks, gifted by the late Dr. Peter Lynch, it is apparent that figures like Kyrle, Pinkus, and Paul Unna, among many others, significantly contributed to the foundational clinical and subsequent histopathologic knowledge that still forms the basis of dermatopathology in the 21st century. Dr. Paul Unna is particularly memorable; a photograph of him hangs in my office. During his time in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, Dr. Unna was regarded as among the very top dermatologists globally, trained in Vienna and practicing in Hamburg. He was the first to describe the stratum granulosum, seborrheic dermatitis (originally known as Unna's disease), acanthosis nigricans, and a variant of congenital patterned nevus (Unna's nevus). His name most frequently arises in modern dermatology clinics when an Unna boot is prescribed. My own English-language experience in dermatopathology can be traced to textbooks by Dr. Walter Leaver.

segments.transcript: Major criteria for dysplastic nevus include a lentiginous or epithelioid proliferation of atypical melanocytes, with a key requirement for cytologic atypia. These are either junctional or superficial compound melanocytic nevi. When a junctional component is present, there is a shoulder, meaning that at the periphery of the lesion, the junctional component extends peripherally beyond the central dermal component, with three rete ridges being an approximate rule of thumb. Minor criteria are mostly architectural and include fusion and bridging of rete ridges, associated lamellar or concentric fibrosis surrounding the bridged rete ridges and associated junctional nests, and an inflammatory host response. Adjacent rete ridges show melanocytes exhibiting cytologic atypia, with nuclei interpreted as hyperchromatic and displaying pleomorphism or variability in shape within the nest. The overall size of these nuclei is comparable to the nuclei in the overlying keratinocytes, all attributes constituting atypia in the context of a dysplastic nevus. Additionally, lamellar concentric fibrosis surrounds the affected melanocytic nests and rete ridges.

Unfortunately, acral melanomas tend to be detected at a later stage, given the greater difficulty in examining acral sites.
