segments.transcript: Desmoplastic melanoma is one of the prototypical 'melanoma wolves in sheep's clothing' at both clinical and histologic levels. Clinically, these are often amelanotic tumors, not even suspected of being melanocytic. Microscopically, a variety of tricky features are observed. While changes of melanoma in situ overlying an invasive melanoma are expected, Desmoplastic melanoma may present with a non-specific lentiginous or junctional proliferation, or even no in situ component. The tumor cells are also microscopically amelanotic, often appearing as bland spindle cells, sometimes mimicking a scar, especially in partial biopsies. Desmoplastic melanoma clinically occurs in high cumulative sun damage areas, though the invasive component of acral melanoma can also be desmoplastic. At the molecular level, these tumors are unique, characterized by a high mutation burden and UV signature mutations, particularly in head and neck tumors. Asymmetry, which includes the host response, can be assessed by drawing an imaginary line through the middle of the lesion and seeing if it looks the same on both sides or different. Pagetoid growth or pagetoid upward scatter is characterized by melanocytes present as single or nested clustered units above the basal layer. Melanocytes can typically be identified at the stage of Melanoma In Situ (MIS) based on cytologic atypia or characteristic cytoplasmic features. segments.transcript: Chondrodermatitis Nodularis Helicis (CNH) is attributable to a disorder of one or more connective tissues, primarily the cartilage of the ear, sometimes associated with abnormalities of elastin in the form of solar elastosis. CNH may be multifactorial, with a role for chronic pressure or irritation in addition to abnormalities reflected by the adjacent or overlying elastic tissue. From a dermatopathologist's perspective, typical shave biopsies usually do not go deep enough to visualize the underlying cartilage, though it is not required for diagnosis. In practical terms, sufficient tissue is needed to rule out squamous cell carcinoma or, to a lesser extent, actinic keratosis. These shave biopsies typically show associated epidermal hyperplasia flanking a central ulcer with crust. The hyperplastic epidermis resembles acral skin or prurigo nodularis; thus, one may see hair follicles on the ear, sometimes referred to as the hairy palm sign associated with prurigo nodularis. CNH can be thought of as prurigo nodularis on the ear. Other distinctive features include prominent fibrin at the junction or base of the central ulcer, which can be seen in initial images and allows for the suspicion of CNH. If a biopsy is from the ear and exhibits these features, CNH is the most likely diagnosis. At closer view, very prominent junctional fibrin is observed at the ulcer base, which, anecdotally, seems quite disproportionate to a run-of-the-mill excoriated nodule.

Chronic GVHD can be divided into lichenoid and sclerodermoid subsets, both clinically and histologically. It can also be classified as interface dermatitis. With multiple neurofibromas, or even a single plexiform neurofibroma, NF1 should be considered. The commonly encountered conventional small neurofibromas have no distinctive histologic features, whether they be sporadic or NF1 associated. However, some other patterns are unique; diffuse neurofibroma and plexiform neurofibroma have distinctive appearances. In contrast to the commonly encountered polypoid and buttonhole papules of common neurofibromas, diffuse neurofibroma presents as a plaque and can resemble dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans in its extensive infiltration and entrapment of subcutaneous fat cells. Plexiform neurofibroma is regarded as pathognomonic for NF1 and is characterized by multiple large, well-demarcated nodules resembling large nerve trunks. Additionally, Schwann cells and variable numbers of axons are demarcated by a perineural sheath, together forming a plexiform pattern of growth that resembles a 'bag of worms' upon gross examination. Malignant Peripheral Nerve Sheath Tumor (MPNST), the malignant counterpart of neurofibroma, disproportionately affects patients with NF1. We expect to see atypia and increased mitotic activity. As a rule, MPNST does not arise primarily within the skin, but more likely from underlying soft tissue. segments.transcript: Spindle cell/pleomorphic lipomas are histologically distinctive and benign tumors. Classically, they arise on the upper back, neck, or shoulder area of an adult man; historically, if the tumor was not in this clinical setting, the diagnosis was questioned. Nowadays, it is recognized to occur in women as well as men, with variants involving the extremities and even confined to the dermis reported. There are a couple of buzzwords for this diagnosis, particularly among dermatopathologists in America: a "school of fish" pattern of spindle cell growth and associated thick, ropy or wirey collagen fibers that stand out amidst the spindle cell proliferation and are typically larger and more birefringent. The immunophenotype is distinctive: CD34 positive, S100 negative (in contrast to normal adipocytes), and more recently, these tumors have been shown to be deficient in retinoblastoma (Rb) protein expression. The fat and spindle cell ratio can vary significantly, leading to low-fat and even fat-free variants. Historically, spindle cell lipoma and pleomorphic lipoma were separated, but they have recently been lumped together due to their overlapping histologic and molecular features. Spindle cell lipoma features bland, monomorphous spindle cells within a variably myxoid stroma, often organized in a swirling or whorled pattern resembling a school of fish.

segments.transcript: Regarding drug reactions, it is important to note that while eosinophils are often sought to support a diagnosis, they are not a requirement for a drug reaction to be present; clinical confirmation is essential. Similarly, deep dermal involvement of the inflammatory infiltrate is not required, though it can be a supportive finding. There is also some evidence to suggest that the inflammation in drug reactions might have a predilection for the eccrine unit. In this anecdotal example of a clinically confirmed trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (Septra/Bactrim)-induced drug reaction, we see spongiotic dermatitis. There are a lot of extravasated erythrocytes, so perhaps this is a purpuric drug reaction. While eosinophils are not abundant, they are present. Histologic features of venous stasis, in addition to the somewhat restrictive clinical setting, include a distinctive combination of findings: extravasated red blood cells, subsequent deposition of hemosiderin and siderophages, and most characteristically, vascular changes with a pattern of clusters of small, thick-walled vessels. The term nodular angioplasia has been used by some to describe these clusters of small blood vessels. segments.transcript: Organizing pneumonia presents acutely or subacutely with patients experiencing shortness of breath over days to weeks. CT scans typically reveal patchy opacifications that can be migratory over the course of a month, moving to different spots. Rarely, radiologists identify an 'atoll sign,' where the opacification resembles a volcanic atoll, which can be a helpful diagnostic indicator. The pathology findings consistently mirror the CT findings, with opacification often equating to the filling of alveolar spaces. Often, when we see cases, it looks as though something gets damaged, like a pneumonia, and then gets cleaned up or organized. The body's method of cleaning things up is granulation tissue, composed of fibroblasts and small vessels with some inflammatory cells, repairing what's been damaged. This process is observed throughout the body.

A ball of granulation tissue shows elongated or stellate fibroblasts within a myxoid background. This bluish myxoid color often helps recognize organizing pneumonia within an airway, which does not cause luminal narrowing. The peripheral smooth muscle of the airway maintains its total diameter, despite the filling of the space. This condition was previously called bronchiolitis obliterans organizing pneumonia (BOOP) due to the appearance of space obliteration; however, it is not true bronchiolitis obliterans, so it is now simply referred to as organizing pneumonia. When viewed distally through the alveolar tissue, polypoid plugs of granulation tissue fill the air spaces, recognizable by their rounded or branching quality and the bluish appearance of the myxoid tissue.

segments.transcript: Acute lung injury is a broad category that clinicians often use synonymously or interchangeably with acute respiratory distress syndrome. In pathology, various types of acute lung injury are discussed, with the usual histology involving diffuse alveolar damage and its associated changes. This can also include airspace organization, organizing pneumonia, and the category of fibrinous organizing pneumonia. Pathology should mirror clinical and radiologic findings, emphasizing the importance of not misinterpreting biopsy artifacts like fibrin as diffuse alveolar damage without proper clinical context. It is crucial to review clinical history and imaging, as misdiagnosing conditions like diffuse alveolar hemorrhage based on isolated findings can erode clinician trust. In acute lung injury, there is damage to the alveolar unit. As termed by Liebow, diffuse alveolar damage signifies damage affecting both the endothelial capillary cells and the epithelial type one or type two pneumocytes within the alveolar unit. The lung tissue becomes leaky, leading to airspace fluid, protein, and fibrin accumulation, and the formation of hyaline membranes from dead epithelial cells. This initiates a vicious cycle of stretch injury, particularly when the patient is attempting to breathe or is mechanically ventilated.

segments.transcript: This slide, which Kevin Leslie took from Anna Katzinskine's book, illustrates these progressive changes. First, damage to the alveolar unit leads to increased edema, followed by cell death and the epithelial component, with a mixture of nucleoplasm, cytoplasm, and fibrin making hyaline membranes. This peaks around day two. Then, incoming cells react to and clean things up; this is the inflammatory or organizational period. This is followed by fibroplasia, which could manifest as organizing pneumonia, resembling granulation tissue that cleans up fibrosis and then undergoes apoptosis and disappears. Alternatively, it could be what is observed in some long COVID patients: diffuse alveolar damage followed by a fibrotic, non-specific interstitial pneumonia with diffuse alveolar septal fibrosis. These diverse changes can sometimes make recognition difficult for a pathologist. It should be noted that the extent of fibroplasia has significantly decreased since around the year 2000 with the advent of ARDSNet, which decreased ventilator pressures. The previous practice of driving oxygen into dead space to open alveoli, resulting in stretch injury, was found to cause more harm than good. With the decreased pressures used in ARDSNet settings, less fibroplasia is now observed.

Jean Olson, the old renal pathologist that was here, used to describe this 'water white' appearance when there was an expansion of interstitial space with insufficient protein to take up the stain, indicating edema. This edema causes thickening of the alveolar septum. In addition, there is a plastering of pinkish material on the surface, which might initially be considered fibrin. However, if you perform a stain like phosphotungstic acid hematoxylin (PTAH) for fibrin, it won't stain significantly; a keratin stain, however, often will. The reason for this is that hyaline membranes, despite appearing as a homogeneous pink substance, are composed of a 'ground-up sausage' of dead cells. They consist of nucleoplasm, cytoplasm, fibrin, and a little bit of protein, stuck onto the surface of the alveolar unit. This represents evidence of acute lung injury, specifically early acute lung injury with edema formation and hyaline membranes. As the condition progresses, these hyaline membranes persist, perhaps with a more pronounced coloration.

segments.transcript: On this slide, we observe various cells moving into the tissue, including neutrophils and mature-looking lymphocytes coursing through, and possibly a few monocytes or histiocytes cleaning up. Researchers often observe a significant release of neutrophils in diffuse alveolar damage, especially when performing washes. However, pathologists do not typically see a large number of neutrophils in generic diffuse alveolar damage. Neutrophils are notably increased in cases caused by infection or sepsis. Cases of transfusion-related acute lung injury often show histologically visible neutrophils. Trauma cases can also strangely exhibit numerous neutrophils, and in some rejection cases, numerous neutrophils can be present. Thus, while more prevalent in research findings, these cells are present for cleanup. This histology micrograph, stained with H&E, demonstrates how the tissue becomes consolidated. If we trace along the alveolar septal surface, we can see that the septa are markedly thickened. The lung has become consolidated, appearing more solid due to polypoid plugs of granulation tissue that are now filling the air spaces. While this might resemble generic organizing pneumonia, it is not classified solely as such due to extensive septal destruction. Instead, this represents organizing acute lung injury or organizing diffuse alveolar damage with organizing pneumonia. This pathology is in the consolidated or fibroplasia stage, where reparative phenomena begin to appear, including these characteristic polypoid plugs of granulation tissue.

As inflammation begins to resolve, fibroplasia occurs, contributing to further cleanup. Ideally, these fibroblasts undergo apoptosis and disappear, leaving the patient with good lung function. Alternatively, if the septa become fibrotic instead of the air spaces, patients may develop chronic disease resulting from diffuse alveolar damage, representing a fibrotic stage of diffuse alveolar damage. segments.transcript: Clues for diffuse alveolar damage when making this pathological diagnosis include a compatible clinical history, relatively acute onset of shortness of breath, diffuse alveolar septal thickening or effacement by collapse, edema, and alveolar filling predominantly with fibrin and proteinaceous fluid, along with hyaline membrane formation. Hyaline membrane is the diagnostic feature for diffuse alveolar damage; without it, it's often termed an acute lung injury pattern. Distal airways and alveolar ducts may show squamous metaplastic change, sometimes with neutrophils. It's crucial not to misinterpret squamous metaplasia in a bronchial wash from a patient with diffuse alveolar damage as cancer. If diffuse alveolar damage presents with eosinophils, one possibility is acute eosinophilic pneumonia, a clinical term often linked to cigarette smoking, particularly seen in soldiers during Southwest Asian conflicts who started smoking. Other causes include drug reactions, certain infections (usually fungal), and parasitic infections. In acute eosinophilic pneumonia, eosinophils may not be immediately obvious; the presence of fibrin and macrophages in air spaces should prompt a high-power examination for them. Eosinophils can be subtle or lysed if the patient has received steroids, leaving behind hyper-eosinophilic granular fibrin. Less common causes include rheumatoid arthritis concerns and Churg-Strauss syndrome, now known as eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

segments.transcript: Cases of Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA) are identifiable using helpful tests like the ELISA for Proteinase 3 (PR3)-ANCA antibody (C-ANCA) in patients with suspicious findings. Patients usually present with kidney, sinonasal, or pulmonary abnormalities, which may include coughing blood, recurrent nosebleeds, or kidney failure. Typically, CAT scans reveal multiple cavitary lesions; a solitary lesion is unusual for GPA. Histologically, GPA involves necrotizing vasculitis and granulomatous inflammation, which is a histiocyte-rich inflammatory infiltrate, but notably, not well-formed granulomas. If well-formed granulomas are present, infection should be considered over GPA. Microscopic examination often shows a central area of blue necrosis, palisading histiocytes at the periphery, and giant cells with closely packed, angular, hyperchromatic nuclei. Another common feature is neutrophilic micro-abscesses, considered an early form of geographic necrosis seen in GPA. Vasculitis should be observed in these cases, if possible.

segments.transcript: This case shows a bronchovascular bundle in the center, with an interlobular septum. There is a vague accentuation of inflammation around the central area. The alveolar septa are thickened by a lymphocytic inflammatory component, indicating too many inflamed cells with a bronchiole-eccentric pattern. In the interstitium, aggregates of histiocytes are observed, some with purple calcifications known as Schaumann bodies, and others with cholesterol clefts—elongated, tiny needle-shaped or acicular clefts within the cytoplasm. This appearance of lymphocytic inflammation with bronchiole-eccentric accentuation and poorly formed granulomas, often with a few or even a single giant cell, is the classical presentation of hypersensitivity pneumonia resulting from inhaled antigens causing a lymphocytic reaction. The usual culprits for hypersensitivity pneumonia are birds, bird dander from powder down feathers, and molds. Hypersensitivity pneumonia is characterized by interstitial chronic inflammation with bronchiocentric accentuation, poorly formed granulomas, and foci of organizing pneumonia. In the current pathologic classification, it has again been defined as a triad, with bronchiolocentric inflammation and organizing pneumonia grouped as bronchiolitis, alongside granulomas and interstitial inflammation. The composition of this classical triad often seems to change.

segments.transcript: Soft findings in granulomas present distinct patterns that aid diagnosis. Tightly packed, coalescing granulomas along lymphatic roots with excluded lymphocytes are characteristic of sarcoidosis. When granulomas are tightly packed singletons with lymphocytes percolating through their center, found in air spaces and interstitium, they are often seen in infectious diseases, particularly Mycobacterium Avium Complex (MAC) and conditions like hot-tub lung. Loose aggregates of macrophages, sometimes containing intracytoplasmic cholesterol clefts within the interstitium, indicate hypersensitivity pneumonitis (HP). Lastly, large, floppy, multinucleated macrophages, often described as foreign body giant cells, are a clue for aspiration, frequently associated with neutrophils and possibly forming a 'pedal sign'.

segments.transcript: Here is the classical lymphatic distribution of sarcoidosis. We observe rounded granulomas closely following the lymphatic routes, specifically within the bronchovascular bundle, nestled between the bronchus and the artery. This illustrates the proper lymphatic distribution of granulomas, which can be seen pushing lymphocytes to the side. This presentation is also evident in the subpleural region and extending along the interlobular septum. In the sub-epithelial space, the case initially appears to be sarcoidosis, as it is a perfect mimic: chronic beryllium disease of the lung. This condition is an immune reaction occurring after exposure to beryllium or similar metals, causing a sarcoid-like reaction. This phenomenon is one reason why sarcoidosis is believed to be an inhalational antigen-driven disease. In this second case, granulomas are arranged as single rounded areas. Upon zooming in, they appear bluer than those observed in sarcoid cases. Hot-tub lung is characterized by lymphocytes intermingling with granulomas, representing a reaction of the lungs to inhaled antigens from *Mycobacterium avium*. This bacterium colonizes the water jets in indoor hot tubs; outdoor hot tubs typically do not concentrate the antigen enough to cause this problem, instead often leading to typical hypersensitivity pneumonitis from mold. A key diagnostic clue for hot-tub lung is that the granulomas will spill into the air spaces.
